fields.title: The Key Teachings of A. B. Simpson
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of A. B. Simpson's message — the Fourfold Gospel of Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King, and the single theme beneath it all: not the blessing but the Blesser, Christ Himself. Eighteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Simpson's own public-domain works — which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by A. B. Simpson. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into eighteen short chapters for the ordinary reader.

Simpson's one theme was Christ Himself. Behind the Fourfold Gospel — Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King — lay a single discovery he never tired of pressing: that the Christian life is not the pursuit of a blessing, an experience or a gift, but the possession of a Person. Once it was the blessing, he sang, now it is the Lord. This volume follows that thread through his life, his deeper-life teaching, and his understanding of faith, prayer and mission, and it ends each chapter where he would have wanted it to end: in a few questions and a prayer.

Simpson's own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, the Bible Simpson preached from, and makes no claim to stand in for the man's own unhurried, Christ-filled pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Where there is neither Greek nor Jew …but Christ is all, and in all. COLOSSIANS 3:11

Among the men whose names are attached to the deeper-life movement, A. B. Simpson is the one most likely to be unfamiliar to the reader, and the one whose fingerprints are most widely distributed. He founded a worldwide missionary movement that now numbers in the millions. He established the first Bible institute in North America, and the pattern he invented has been copied on every continent. He wrote around a hundred books and more than a hundred hymns. He shaped, directly or at one remove, the theology of a great deal of twentieth-century evangelical devotion — A. W. Tozer was his spiritual son and wrote his biography. And most Christians who have absorbed his emphases have never heard his name.

A summary in four words

Simpson’s teaching is unusually easy to summarise, because he summarised it himself. He called it the Fourfold Gospel, and he preached it for forty years: Christ our Saviour. Christ our Sanctifier. Christ our Healer. Christ our Coming King. The structure matters less than what it is built to do. Notice that all four begin with the same word. Simpson was not offering four doctrines but one Person in four relations, and this was the whole point. When a prominent healing evangelist once invited him to spend himself on a nationwide healing campaign, Simpson replied that he had four wheels on his chariot and could not neglect three of them to devote himself to one. That instinct — for wholeness, for keeping things in proportion, for refusing to make any single emphasis the whole — is his most valuable characteristic, and it is what makes him worth reading in an age of ministries built on one idea.

Himself, not it

But beneath the four wheels lies something simpler still, and it is the reason Simpson belongs in this series. His most quoted hymn opens by describing a change he had passed through: that once it had been the blessing, and now it was the Lord; once the feeling, and now the Word; once His gifts he wanted, and now the Giver alone. The hymn is called Himself, and the title is the whole of his theology. Simpson had spent years pursuing spiritual experiences — a deeper consecration, a fuller blessing, the power he saw in others — and had found that each arrival was followed by a fresh emptiness. What broke the cycle was the discovery that Christ does not primarily give things. Christ gives Himself, and everything else is contained in Him.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. EPHESIANS 1:3

That is the thread running through all eighteen chapters of this book, and it is the question to keep asking as you read: am I seeking something from Him, or am I seeking Him?

How this book is arranged

Eighteen short chapters set out his teaching, beginning with that central emphasis, moving through the four wheels of the chariot, then into his teaching on the self life and the Christ life, the Holy Spirit, faith and prayer, and finally to the two things that consumed the last half of his life: the forgotten poor at his door, and the unreached nations beyond the sea. Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Simpson would have insisted on it. He had no patience with truth that stopped at the understanding, and he measured every doctrine by whether it produced a changed life and a worker sent out. Read one chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own.

One more thing must be said at the outset, and it is better said plainly. This is not a book of hero-worship, and there are places where Simpson must be read with care. His teaching on divine healing has been a blessing to many and has done real damage to others. Simpson himself, after his own healing in 1881, set aside medical treatment entirely and taught others to trust Christ alone for the body. Some of those who followed him died of treatable conditions. Some were told, or concluded, that their continued illness proved a deficiency of faith — a cruelty that has crushed sincere believers ever since. Chapter four sets out what he taught, what is genuinely biblical in it, and where it must be qualified. Please read that chapter with its cautions rather than without them. His doctrine of sanctification as a definite second crisis, received by faith after conversion, is held by many godly Christians and rejected by many others who read the same passages differently. This book presents it as he taught it and notes honestly where the disagreement lies. And his expectation that the gospel might be carried to every nation within his own generation, hastening the Lord’s return, proved mistaken — as every such expectation has. The burden was right. The timetable was not. Why read him at all, then? Because on the central matter he was profoundly right, and because he lived what he taught at considerable cost. He walked away from the most comfortable pulpits available to a man of his gifts, twice, to work among people nobody else wanted. He gave away money he needed. He sent out hundreds of missionaries to places from which many did not return, and he buried his own children. So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Weigh every chapter against the Word of God. Where Simpson is faithful — and on the all-sufficiency of Christ, on the indwelling Spirit, on the missionary obligation of the whole church, he is faithful indeed — receive it gladly and act upon it. Where he presses beyond what is written, mark it, set it aside, and lose nothing.

A final word about the reader this book assumes. Simpson wrote for late nineteenth-century North Americans, in a city filling with immigrants, at a moment when the modern missionary movement was gathering force. He is read now in places he prayed for and never saw. The movement he founded is today far larger outside the country he worked in than within it, which would have delighted him and not surprised him at all. He assumed no particular setting, because his subject was not a culture but a Person. Wherever this book is opened, and into whatever language it is carried, the question it presses will already be waiting.

fields.title: A Man with Four Wheels on His Chariot
fields.body_html:
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. PHILIPPIANS 4:13

A Scottish covenanting home. Albert Benjamin Simpson was born on the fifteenth of December, 1843, at Bayview on Prince Edward Island, off the eastern coast of Canada. His parents, James and Janet Simpson, were Scottish, Presbyterian, and severe in the old covenanting way. His father was a shipbuilder and merchant and an elder in the church; the Sabbath was kept without compromise and the catechism was learned. A depression struck the maritime trade in the late 1840s, the family business failed, and they moved west to Chatham in Ontario. The boy grew up in a home of reduced circumstances, religious discipline and considerable anxiety. He was a nervous, conscientious child, and his religion made him miserable. He believed the doctrines and could not find peace in them, and he wore himself into a physical collapse trying. It was the first of several breakdowns that would mark his life.

The first good work. Relief came through a book. In his fifteenth year, during a season of revival in Chatham under the preaching of a visiting Irish evangelist, he came upon Walter Marshall’s old Puritan treatise The Gospel Mystery of Sanctification, and read a sentence that undid the knot: that the first good work a man will ever perform is to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. He had been trying to produce a fitness to come. He saw that believing was the coming. He did not receive a rush of feeling — he was honest about that all his life — but he became settled that Christ had received him. In January 1861 he wrote out a formal covenant giving himself to God, and signed it. He entered Knox College, Toronto, and graduated in 1865.

Three prestigious pulpits. What followed was a career of relentless external success and quiet internal dissatisfaction. At twenty-one he was called to Knox Presbyterian Church in Hamilton, Ontario, one of the largest congregations in Canada. He married Margaret Henry two days after his ordination examinations, and was back in his pulpit the following Sunday. He worked ferociously and added some seven hundred members in eight years.

The Hamilton years also brought the first grief. Their second son, Melville Jennings, died at three years old. Simpson wrote afterwards that until then he had gone to bereaved families with sympathy that was honestly meant and touched nothing, because he had no acquaintance with sorrow of his own. Two of their six children were buried young. In December 1873 he moved to Chestnut Street Presbyterian in Louisville, Kentucky, the leading Presbyterian pulpit in that city. There he pressed for united evangelistic meetings across the denominations, and built a plain tabernacle so that working men who owned no good clothes could come without embarrassment. It succeeded, and his congregation was not entirely pleased. In 1879 he was called to Thirteenth Street Presbyterian Church in New York City, and arrived to find the thing that would define the rest of his life: hundreds of thousands of immigrants pouring into a city whose respectable churches had no intention of receiving them.

Two crises. Two experiences turned him, and they came five years apart. The first was in 1874, at Louisville. Exhausted and conscious that his ministry ran on his own strength, he read W. E. Boardman’s The Higher Christian Life and came into what he afterwards described as the reception of Christ as his sanctification — not a new effort but a new dependence. He dated his real ministry from it. The second was in the summer of 1881. He had been ill for years with a heart condition; a physician in New York had given him three months. At the conference grounds at Old Orchard Beach in Maine he heard Dr Charles Cullis teach on divine healing, and was more struck by the testimonies than the argument. On a Friday afternoon in August he went alone into the pine woods and made a threefold pledge: that he accepted the Bible’s teaching that Jesus is the healer of the body; that he took Him then and there as his own physical life for all the needs of his body until his life-work was done; and that he would use the strength given him for the glory of God and the service of others. He came out of the woods changed. The following day he climbed a mountain of three thousand feet. He lived another thirty-eight years, and worked at a pace that exhausted much younger men.

The break. That autumn he asked his congregation to receive a group of Italian immigrant converts into membership. They declined. In November 1881 he resigned — a settled salary, a distinguished pulpit, and the denomination in which he had been raised and ordained — with no congregation, no income, and seven children. He was baptised by immersion in a Baptist church in New York early the following year. He began preaching in a hall to a handful of people. Within a few years the Gospel Tabernacle was one of the most vigorous congregations in the city, and it was doing what nobody else was doing: rescue missions, work among the poor, an orphanage, homes where the sick could stay and be prayed for, and services for immigrants in their own languages.

Institutions built to send people away. In 1882 he opened a missionary training school — the first Bible institute in North America — on the conviction that ordinary believers with practical training and a call could be got to the field in two years rather than seven. It later moved up the Hudson to Nyack. Nearly every Bible college in the world descends from that idea. At Old Orchard in 1887 he founded two societies: the Christian Alliance, for the deepening of spiritual life at home, and the Evangelical Missionary Alliance, to send workers abroad. In 1897 they merged into The Christian and Missionary Alliance. He never intended a denomination. He wanted a movement inside the existing churches — a fellowship of people from every tradition united by the Fourfold Gospel and the evangelisation of the world. It became a denomination anyway, which is what usually happens. Meanwhile he edited a weekly magazine for nearly forty years, wrote around a hundred books including a commentary on the whole Bible, and composed more than a hundred hymns, often producing the words on Saturday for the congregation to sing on Sunday.

The Pentecostal question. After 1906 the Pentecostal revival swept through the movements nearest to his own, and many Alliance people were caught up in it. Simpson’s response was characteristically balanced and satisfied nobody entirely. He longed for more of the Spirit’s power, and in August 1907 returned to the same pine woods at Old Orchard to ask God for a fuller baptism. He did not speak in tongues, then or later. He concluded that tongues is a genuine gift which God distributes as He wills, and that it is not the necessary evidence of the Spirit’s fullness — and he set the policy that has marked the Alliance since: seek not, forbid not. The cost was real. The movement lost members in both directions, to those who wanted more and to those who wanted the door shut.

The end. His last years were hard. He grew frail, his memory failed, and he passed through a period of spiritual darkness that his friends found painful to watch in a man who had taught so many others about victory. He stepped back from leadership in 1918. He went into a coma on the twenty-eighth of October, 1919, and died the following day at Nyack, aged seventy-five. He left no fortune. He left a training school, a magazine, a hymnbook, a tabernacle full of poor people, and several hundred missionaries scattered across the world in places he had never seen and had prayed for by name.

fields.title: Himself
fields.body_html:
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are complete in him. COLOSSIANS 2:9–10

Simpson wrote a hymn which is still sung in places that have forgotten who wrote it, and its title is a single word: Himself. The verses trace a movement. They describe a man who once sought the blessing and now seeks the Lord; who once lived on feelings and now rests on the Word; who once wanted the gifts and now wants only the Giver; who once was always asking and now is always praising. Each verse makes the same turn — from something Christ provides to Christ Himself. It is autobiography. And it is the key to everything else in this book.

The exhausting pursuit of it

Simpson had spent his early ministry in a condition that many earnest Christians will recognise immediately. He was successful. He was orthodox. He worked to the point of physical collapse — more than once. And he was aware that something was missing, and set about looking for it in the way conscientious people do: by seeking a further experience. A deeper consecration. A fuller blessing. The power he could see in others and could not find in himself. The trouble with this pursuit is that each arrival is followed by a fresh emptiness. You obtain the blessing, and within weeks you need another. Your Christian life becomes a series of peaks with lengthening valleys between them, and your spiritual health comes to depend on how recently you were last at a convention. Simpson’s escape from this was not a better experience. It was the discovery that he had been asking for the wrong category of thing altogether.

Christ does not primarily give things

The insight, once stated, seems almost too simple to have cost so much. Christ does not chiefly dispense blessings, as a benefactor distributes gifts from a store. He gives Himself, and every blessing is contained within Him rather than handed out beside Him.

But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

Read that slowly. Paul does not say Christ gives us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He says Christ is made unto us these things. They are not commodities He supplies; they are what He is to us. To have Him is to have them, and to seek them apart from Him is to look for light somewhere other than the sun.

And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace. JOHN 1:16

Simpson’s whole Fourfold Gospel rests on this. He did not preach salvation, sanctification, healing and the second coming as four topics. He preached Christ our Saviour, Christ our Sanctifier, Christ our Healer, Christ our Coming King — four relations to one Person. Take away the Person and you are left with four doctrines, which is a different and much poorer thing.

The test

There is a question Simpson’s teaching puts to a believer, and it is not comfortable. Suppose God gave you nothing further as long as you live. No answered prayer you are currently waiting on. No relief from the circumstance that is grinding you. No further usefulness, no growth you can detect, no experience to report. Would Christ Himself still be enough?

Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. PSALM 73:25

Most of us discover, asking that honestly, that a good deal of what we call love for God is love for what He does for us — and that our devotion rises and falls with His recent performance. That discovery is not a reason for despair. It is the beginning of the change Simpson’s hymn describes. He was careful to add that this does not make the blessings unimportant. God gives real gifts and means them to be enjoyed. The question is one of order. Seek the gift and you may get it and remain empty; seek the Giver and the gifts arrive as part of the package, held loosely, no longer able to make or break you.

But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. MATTHEW 6:33

Where this leaves the restless

The practical relief in this teaching is considerable, and it is why Simpson mattered so much to the exhausted.

If what you need is an experience, then you must keep obtaining it, and you are permanently vulnerable — to your temperament, your health, your circumstances, the quality of last Sunday’s meeting. If what you need is a Person, and that Person indwells you and has promised never to leave, then your supply does not fluctuate even when your sense of it does.

For he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. HEBREWS 13:5

Simpson taught believers to stop asking for more of the Holy Spirit and to start recognising how much of them the Holy Spirit had. The problem was never the supply.

There is a way to test whether this has moved from theory into practice, and it takes about a week to apply. Listen to your own praying. Count how much of it asks Christ for something, and how much of it simply wants Him. Most of us find the second column almost empty, and we have been calling the first column a devotional life.

Leanness of soul

There is a verse in the Psalms which describes the danger of getting what you asked for, and Simpson returned to it often.

And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul. PSALM 106:15

Israel in the wilderness wanted meat. They complained until they got it. God granted the petition exactly as made, and something was lost in the granting that they had not thought to protect. The warning is not that God punishes us for asking. It is that a request granted on our own terms may leave us thinner than we were, because what we actually needed was not the thing but the God who was withholding it, and we were too busy negotiating to notice. Simpson applied this directly to the pursuit of spiritual experiences. fields.body_html:
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. ACTS 4:12

The first wheel of the chariot is the one every Christian assumes he has already understood, and Simpson’s treatment of it is worth attention precisely because of how he came to it.

A boy who could not get in

He was raised in a rigorous Scottish Presbyterian home, catechised thoroughly, and made thoroughly wretched by it. He believed every doctrine he had been taught. He could not find peace in any of them. The difficulty was not intellectual. It was that he understood himself to be required to arrive at some condition — sufficient repentance, adequate sorrow, a certain quality of surrender — before he could come to Christ. And every time he examined himself he found the condition unmet. He drove himself into a physical collapse trying to produce it. What released him, at fifteen, was a sentence in an old Puritan book: that the first good work a man will ever perform is to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. He saw it. He had been trying to become fit to come, and the coming was the fitness. There was nothing to bring.

But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

He was honest all his life that no great emotion accompanied this. He simply took what was offered, and afterwards became settled that Christ had received him. Feelings came later, and irregularly, and he never allowed them to be the foundation.

More than pardon

But Simpson’s distinctive emphasis lies elsewhere, and it shapes everything that follows in his teaching. Salvation, as he preached it, is not merely the cancelling of a debt. It is the impartation of a life.

He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life. 1 JOHN 5:12

A man may be forgiven and remain what he was. If salvation were pardon only, the sinner would leave the courtroom acquitted and unchanged, facing the same future with the same nature. What Scripture describes is birth — a new category of existence, with a life in it that was not there before.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

This is why Simpson could move so naturally from the first wheel to the second. If salvation is the impartation of Christ’s life, then sanctification is not a separate programme requiring different machinery. It is the same life, further received.

Christ our salvation, not merely its author

Notice the grammar of the Fourfold Gospel again. Not Christ the giver of salvation, but Christ our Saviour — and Simpson pressed even that into the possessive.

The Lord is my strength and song, and is become my salvation. EXODUS 15:2

Is become my salvation. Not has provided it. The Old Testament says this repeatedly, and Simpson would not let the phrase be flattened into a figure of speech. Christ does not stand outside us holding our salvation; He enters, and is it. The practical difference shows up when a believer sins. If salvation is a thing you were given, then failure raises the question of whether you still have it, and the anxious conscience spends its life auditing. If salvation is a Person who has taken up residence, the question changes entirely: not do I still possess it? but is He still there? — and He has answered that Himself.

And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. JOHN 10:28

Free, and therefore urgent

One further note, because it explains the rest of Simpson’s life. The freeness of salvation did not make him casual about it. It made him frantic. A man who believes that salvation must be earned may reasonably conclude that most people will not manage it, and settle into resignation. A man who believes it is free, complete and available to anyone who will simply take it, cannot be calm about the fact that millions have never been told. Simpson’s missionary passion was not a separate enthusiasm bolted onto his theology. It was the direct consequence of what he believed about grace.

How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? ROMANS 10:14

If you have carried a quiet suspicion that you must reach some standard before God will fully receive you, the sentence that freed a miserable fifteen-year-old in Ontario is worth sitting with. The first good work you will ever do is to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. Everything else follows. Nothing else precedes.

Assurance without feeling

Simpson’s own conversion supplies a useful lesson for a very common difficulty. He took Christ at fifteen and felt nothing. For some time afterwards he was troubled by the absence, because he had heard others describe a flood of joy at their conversion and could report no such thing. He concluded eventually that he had been looking for evidence in the wrong place. The New Testament grounds assurance not in the quality of an experience but in the reliability of a word.

These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life. 1 JOHN 5:13

John says he wrote so that believers might know — and the instrument of that knowing is the thing written, not the emotion felt. Simpson’s counsel to the anxious was accordingly simple and unromantic. Do not examine your feelings to discover whether you are saved; examine what God has promised to those who come, and then determine whether you have come.

All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

He noticed the double negative in that promise — in no wise — and regarded it as deliberate. The Lord appears to have anticipated exactly the person who would come and then doubt whether he had been received. None of this makes feeling worthless. Simpson had plenty of it later, and wrote hymns out of it. The point is one of foundation: emotion is a good deal more enjoyable than fact and a great deal less reliable, and a house built on it will move whenever its owner is tired, ill or discouraged.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the condition you have been quietly trying to meet before you believe God fully accepts you. Then stop trying to meet it. 2. Check whether your assurance rests on feeling or on what God has said. If feeling, deliberately move the weight. 3. Consider whether you think of salvation as a transaction you received or a Person who lives in you. The second changes how you handle failure. 4. If you have never definitely taken Christ, do it now, in the plainest words you can manage. There is nothing to bring. 5. Let the freeness of the gospel produce urgency rather than complacency. Name one person who has never clearly heard it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have spent years trying to become fit to come to You, and the coming was the fitness all along.
I bring nothing. I have nothing to bring. I take what You have offered because You have offered it, and not because I have qualified.
Be my salvation — not a gift held at a distance, but Yourself living in me.
And having received freely, let me not be calm about those who have never been told. Amen.

fields.title: Christ Our Sanctifier
fields.body_html:
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly …Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:23–24

In 1874, at Louisville, Simpson was pastoring the leading Presbyterian church in the city and was privately at the end of himself. He was working at a pace that would break him, and he knew the work was running on his own resources. He was orthodox, admired and dry. Reading W. E. Boardman’s The Higher Christian Life, he came into what he afterwards called the reception of Christ as his sanctification — and he dated the real beginning of his ministry from it.

Not achievement but reception

The heart of Simpson’s teaching here is contained in a preposition. Most believers approach holiness as something to be achieved. We identify our faults, resolve, apply effort, monitor progress, and fail with tiresome regularity. Sanctification becomes a self-improvement project in religious language, and its characteristic products are exhaustion and pretence. Simpson taught that holiness is to be received, because it is not a quality but a Person.

But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

Christ is our sanctification in exactly the sense that He is our righteousness. We did not manufacture the second and we shall not manufacture the first. The same Christ who was received for pardon is received for holiness, by the same faith, on the same terms.

As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him. COLOSSIANS 2:6

As ye have received — that is, by faith, freely, as a gift. So walk — by the same method, all the way down.

The branch and the vine

Simpson’s governing image, like that of most deeper-life teachers, is the vine.

Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. JOHN 15:4

He drew out the point that a branch does not produce fruit by effort. It bears fruit — which is a passive verb — because sap from another source flows through it. The branch’s whole responsibility is connection. This is not an invitation to inactivity, and Simpson’s own schedule refutes any such reading. He worked harder than almost anyone of his generation. The question is not whether the Christian labours but whose energy the labour runs on.

Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. COLOSSIANS 1:29

Paul labours; he strives; and he does it according to an energy that is not his. Simpson considered that verse the exact description of the sanctified life.

Crisis and process

Here we come to the part of his teaching that is contested, and it should be set out plainly. Simpson held that sanctification involves a definite crisis — a moment at which the believer, having seen his own insufficiency, deliberately hands over the whole of himself and takes Christ by faith as his holiness. He did not regard this as optional or as a refinement for advanced Christians. He thought most believers were living far below their privileges because they had never made that transaction. He was equally clear that the crisis is not the end. What follows is a lifetime of growth, in which the surrender made once must be maintained daily and applied to territory not yet surveyed.

But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. 2 PETER 3:18

Now the honest qualification. Many careful Christians read the New Testament differently. They hold that sanctification begins at conversion and proceeds gradually throughout life, that Scripture nowhere teaches a distinct second crisis, and that Simpson’s framework can leave believers either presuming on an experience they once had or despairing because they cannot locate one. The Reformed tradition in which Simpson himself was raised takes broadly this view. The reader should feel free to weigh it. What is not in dispute — and it is the substance of the chapter — is that holiness is Christ’s work in us rather than our achievement, that it is appropriated by faith rather than manufactured by resolve, and that a great many believers have never definitely handed themselves over at all.

Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God. ROMANS 6:13

Whether that yielding is a crisis or the first of ten thousand small consecrations, it has to happen.

There is a diagnostic in this that anyone can apply. Take the fault you have fought longest — the temper, the tongue, the appetite, the fear. Ask honestly what method you have been using. If the answer is resolution, monitoring and effort, you have been trying to produce what only Christ can be in you. That is not an argument for doing nothing. It is an argument for doing something different.

What it does not mean

Simpson was careful to fence this doctrine, because the language of holiness teaching has been used to claim things Scripture does not. It does not mean sinless perfection. Simpson denied that any believer arrives at a state in which sin is impossible or temptation has no force. He held that the capacity for sin remains, that the believer stands only by continuing dependence, and that anyone who claims otherwise is contradicting the apostle.

If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. 1 JOHN 1:8

It does not mean the eradication of the old nature. What Simpson taught was displacement rather than removal — the indwelling Christ occupying and governing what remains, moment by moment, in the way a stream keeps a channel clean by continuing to flow rather than by the channel being altered. And it does not mean the end of growth. The believer who has made the fullest consecration he knows how to make has surrendered only what he could see at the time. Ten years later God will show him territory he did not know existed, and the same handing over will be required again on new ground.

But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. PROVERBS 4:18

The image is of increasing light, not of arrival. Simpson used it to protect believers from two errors at once: the presumption that says the matter is settled and needs no further attention, and the despair that says nothing has happened because everything has not.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Identify the sin you have fought longest by willpower. Bring it to Christ as something to receive victory in rather than achieve. 2. Make a definite transaction if you never have: hand yourself over, in words, on a date, and tell someone. 3. Examine whose energy your service runs on. Exhaustion and resentment are usually the first symptoms of the wrong answer. 4. Practise abiding concretely: a fixed daily time of conscious dependence before the day’s work rather than after it. 5. Hold this doctrine graciously. Sincere believers differ about the crisis; none differ about the necessity of holiness.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have been trying to produce a holiness that only You can be in me.
I have resolved and failed, resolved and failed, and called the cycle the Christian life. I am tired of it, and I think that is Your mercy.
I hand myself over — not a portion, and not on conditions. Be my sanctification as truly as You are my righteousness.
Keep me abiding. Let the fruit be Yours, and let me stop straining to grow what only sap can produce. Amen.

But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. PROVERBS 4:18 The image is of increasing light, not of arrival. Simpson used it to protect believers from two errors at once: the presumption that says the matter is settled and needs no further attention, and the despair that says nothing has happened because everything has not. Make a definite transaction if you never have: hand yourself over, in words, on a date, and tell someone. 3. Examine whose energy your service runs on. Exhaustion and resentment are usually the first symptoms of the wrong answer. 4. Practise abiding concretely: a fixed daily time of conscious dependence before the day’s work rather than after it. 5. Hold this doctrine graciously. Sincere believers differ about the crisis; none differ about the necessity of holiness. I am tired of it, and I think that is Your mercy. I hand myself over — not a portion, and not on conditions. Be my sanctification as truly as You are my righteousness. Keep me abiding. Let the fruit be Yours, and let me stop straining to grow what only sap can produce. Amen.

fields.title: Christ Our Healer
fields.body_html:
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. JAMES 5:14

This is the most contested wheel of Simpson’s chariot, and it must be handled with more care than any other chapter in this book. Please read the cautions at the end. They are not an afterthought; they are part of the teaching.

The pine woods at Old Orchard

Simpson had been an invalid for much of his adult life. He suffered from a heart condition, had collapsed more than once from overwork, and carried a bottle of medicine with him for the attacks that came when he climbed a flight of stairs. A physician in New York had told him he had about three months. In the summer of 1881, resting at the conference grounds at Old Orchard Beach in Maine, he heard Dr Charles Cullis teach on divine healing. He was less moved by the arguments than by the testimonies of people who had been healed. He went away and studied his New Testament on the subject for himself, and became convinced. On a Friday afternoon in August he walked alone into the pine woods and made a threefold pledge: that he accepted the Bible’s teaching that Jesus heals the body; that he took Christ then and there as his physical life for every need of his body until his life-work was finished; and that he would use the strength given him for the glory of God and the service of others. The next day he climbed a mountain of three thousand feet. Shortly afterwards he prayed for his daughter Margaret, gravely ill with diphtheria — the disease that had killed his young son Melville a decade before — and she recovered. He lived thirty-eight more years himself, and worked at a pace that exhausted much younger men.

What he taught

Simpson set out his position in The Gospel of Healing (1885), and its core is a claim about the atonement.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows …he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. ISAIAH 53:4–5

Matthew quotes the first half of that passage and applies it explicitly to Christ’s healing ministry (Matthew 8:16–17). From this Simpson argued that Christ bore our sicknesses as truly as our sins, and that healing for the body therefore belongs within the provision of the cross rather than outside it. He was careful about what this did not mean. He did not teach that the body is already redeemed — he held firmly that full physical redemption awaits the resurrection. What he claimed was that a measure of resurrection life is available now, to be drawn upon by faith, as strength for the body while the Lord’s work for that person remains unfinished. His own phrasing was that he took Christ as his physical life until all my life-work is done — a qualification that is almost always omitted when he is quoted. He also insisted the doctrine be kept in proportion. When the healing evangelist John Alexander Dowie invited him to devote himself to a nationwide healing campaign, Simpson answered that he had four wheels on his chariot and could not neglect three to concentrate on one. He never allowed healing to become the message.

What is genuinely biblical here

Several things in Simpson’s emphasis are plainly scriptural, and churches that have reacted against the excesses have often lost them. God heals, and He heals today. Nothing in Scripture retires the practice. The church is instructed to pray for the sick, and specifically to anoint them with oil through its elders. James 5 is a standing command that a great many congregations simply ignore.

And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up. JAMES 5:15

The body matters to God. He made it, Christ took one, and it will be raised. A spirituality that treats the body as irrelevant is closer to ancient paganism than to Scripture. And Christ’s compassion for the sick is one of the most conspicuous features of the Gospels. He was repeatedly moved with compassion before He healed anybody.

Where it must be qualified

Now the necessary corrections, and they must be stated without softening, because people have been badly hurt here. Scripture does not promise healing in every case. The New Testament records faithful believers who were not healed. Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Epaphroditus was ill to the point of death (Philippians 2:27). Timothy had a recurring stomach complaint, and Paul’s counsel was not a rebuke about faith but a practical remedy (1 Timothy 5:23). And Paul himself asked three times for the removal of his thorn and was refused.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 CORINTHIANS 12:9

That is God declining to heal an apostle, and calling the refusal grace. Any doctrine that cannot accommodate this verse has a defect. The sick must never be blamed. The teaching that continued illness proves deficient faith is cruel, and it is the error God rebuked in the book of Job. It adds guilt to suffering and drives the afflicted away from the church precisely when they need it. If you have been told your illness is your fault, that was not the mind of Christ toward you. Medicine is not unbelief. Luke, who travelled with Paul, is called the beloved physician. The Samaritan poured oil and wine into wounds. Isaiah applied a poultice of figs to Hezekiah’s boil in the same episode in which God miraculously extended his life. Scripture nowhere treats treatment and trust as rivals. Simpson’s own practice went further than this. After 1881 he set aside medical means entirely for himself and taught others to do the same, and some who followed him died of conditions that could have been treated. This is the point at which he must be respectfully declined. Nothing in this chapter should lead any reader to refuse, delay or discontinue medical care. Pray, and see your physician. And everyone dies. Simpson grew frail, lost his memory, and died at seventy-five. That is not a failure of his doctrine; it is the human condition. The final healing is not in this life.

Even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body. ROMANS 8:23

Held with those corrections, the substance remains and it is worth recovering. Pray boldly for the sick. Obey James 5. Expect God to act, and leave the outcome with Him. And when He does not heal, do not conclude that He has not answered — Paul did not.

How to pray for the sick

A practical note, since the doctrine can leave believers unsure what to actually say at a bedside. Pray boldly. Ask plainly for healing, without hedging every sentence into meaninglessness. The Lord invited direct requests, and the sick person is generally helped by hearing someone ask God for the thing they want.

Pray submissively. The pattern is in Gethsemane, where the Son of God asked for the cup to pass and added a clause.

Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. MATTHEW 26:39

That clause is not weak faith. It is the faith of the One who had more of it than anybody, and it belongs in our praying for the same reason it belonged in His. Promise nothing. Do not tell a sick person that God will certainly heal them in this life. You do not know, and if you are wrong they must bear both the illness and the collapse of what they were told. Stay. The most valuable thing most of us can offer is not a prayer formula but persistence — continuing to visit when the novelty has worn off and the condition has not improved. Job’s friends were at their best in the seven days they sat and said nothing. And pray for more than the body. Ask for endurance, for peace, for the absence of bitterness, for the person’s family. These prayers are always according to God’s will, and they are always answered.

Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. 1 PETER 5:7
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Pray specifically and expectantly for someone who is ill this week, without promising them an outcome God has not promised. 2. If your church never practises James 5:14, ask your leaders why. 3. If you have been made to feel that your illness is a verdict on your faith, reject that. It is not the teaching of Scripture. 4. Take your medicine and keep your appointments. Trust and treatment are not rivals. 5. Sit with 2 Corinthians 12:9 until you can say it about the thing God has not removed from you.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You healed the sick because You were moved with compassion, and You are unchanged.
Teach me to pray boldly for the suffering, without pretending to know what You have not told me.
Where You heal, let me give You the glory. Where You do not, let me hear You say that Your grace is sufficient, and believe it.
And guard me from ever adding to another’s burden by suggesting that their sickness is their own fault. Amen.

fields.title: Christ Our Coming King
fields.body_html:
This same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven. ACTS 1:11

The fourth wheel was, for Simpson, not a speculative appendix but the engine of everything practical he did. He built a training school, founded a missionary society and drove himself into repeated exhaustion because he believed the King was coming and there was work to finish first.

A personal, visible return

His position was straightforward and he defended it against the alternatives current in his day. The return of Christ is personal — this same Jesus, not a principle, an influence, or the gradual improvement of society. It is visible. And it is an event, not a process.

Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him. REVELATION 1:7
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout …and the dead in Christ shall rise first. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:16

Simpson held the premillennial view — that Christ returns before the promised age of righteousness, rather than at the end of a period of gradual Christian progress. This mattered to him practically. The optimistic alternative popular in his generation held that the world was steadily improving and the kingdom was arriving through civilisation and reform. Simpson thought that view drained the urgency out of missions, and the twentieth century did not treat it kindly. Christians differ on the details of the timing, and have since the earliest centuries. What the New Testament asserts without ambiguity is the fact.

Why it is called a blessed hope

Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. TITUS 2:13

Simpson dwelt on the adjective. The return of Christ is not, for the believer, primarily a terror. It is the moment the whole story has been travelling towards: the end of separation, the vindication of everything endured, and the sight of the One we have loved without seeing.

Whom having not seen, ye love …yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 PETER 1:8

He noticed how the New Testament actually deploys this doctrine. It is used to comfort the bereaved, to steady the persecuted, to encourage the labouring, and to sober the careless. It is almost never used to satisfy curiosity.

What the hope produces

Three effects, each with a text. Purity. The expectation of seeing Him has a cleansing force that mere rules do not.

And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure. 1 JOHN 3:3

Watchfulness. Not calculation — watchfulness. The believer lives as a servant whose master may return at any hour, which is a different posture from one who has worked out the schedule.

Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come. MATTHEW 24:42

Urgency in mission. This is the link that governed Simpson’s life, and it comes from the Lord’s own words.

And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come. MATTHEW 24:14

Simpson read that as a task with a stated relation to the return, and it made him incapable of leaving the unreached alone. Every institution he founded was built to get workers to places where Christ had not been named.

Where he was mistaken

Honesty requires a note. Simpson and many of his contemporaries expected that the gospel might reach every nation within their own generation, and that the Lord would then return. That expectation was not fulfilled, and similar expectations have failed in every century since the first. He generally avoided setting dates, and he was more restrained than many around him. But the flavour of imminence in his writing sometimes shades into calculation, and the reader should hold that lightly. The Lord Himself declined to supply the information.

And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power. But ye shall receive power …and ye shall be witnesses unto me. ACTS 1:7–8

Notice how the verse continues. The refusal of the timetable is immediately followed by the commission. That is exactly the right ordering, and it preserves everything valuable in Simpson’s urgency while removing what was mistaken in it.

The practical question is not when He is coming. It is whether you would be glad to be found doing what you are doing when He does.

A doctrine for the grieving

It is worth noticing the setting in which the New Testament’s fullest teaching on the return of Christ appears, because it is not a prophecy conference. Paul is writing to a young church that has buried some of its members and is distressed about them. The question is not chronology. It is whether their dead have missed something.

But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:13

Paul then gives the great passage about the Lord descending with a shout, the dead in Christ rising first, and the living being caught up together with them. And he closes not with an exhortation to watch the signs but with an instruction about pastoral care.

Wherefore comfort one another with these words. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:18

Simpson kept this use of the doctrine prominent, and it is a good test of whether we are handling it as Scripture does. A believer whose interest in the second coming runs entirely to charts and current events has drifted from the apostolic pattern. A believer who can sit with a grieving friend and make the return of Christ a genuine consolation is using it exactly as Paul did. Note also the phrase together with them. The reunion is part of the hope. The Christian’s expectation is not merely that he will see Christ, but that the separations death has caused are temporary.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask whether the return of Christ functions in your life as a doctrine you affirm or a hope you actually anticipate.

2. Apply 1 John 3:3 concretely: name one thing you would want dealt with before He appears, and deal with it. 3. Stop calculating and start watching. If you follow prophetic speculation, consider how much of that time could go to intercession instead. 4. Use this hope the way the New Testament does — to comfort someone bereaved, or to steady someone under pressure. 5. Consider what you are doing that will matter on that day, and do more of it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are coming, and I have arranged my life as though You were not.
Forgive the drowsiness that treats Your return as a doctrine rather than a hope. Make me watchful without making me speculative.
Purify me. Let the thought of seeing You do what rules have never done in me.
And let me be found at work — among the people You died for, in the places where You are not yet named — when You come. Amen.

fields.title: The Self Life and the Christ Life
fields.body_html:
I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. GALATIANS 2:20

One of Simpson’s most searching books carries the title The Self Life and the Christ Life, and its argument is that the Christian’s fundamental problem is not his sins but his self.

The root beneath the branches

Most of us deal with our Christian lives at the level of particular faults. We notice a bad temper, a sharp tongue, a habit of exaggeration, and we address each as it appears — pruning branches, one at a time, for decades. Simpson’s contention is that the branches keep growing because the root is untouched. Beneath the individual sins lies a single organising principle: the self at the centre, arranging everything around its own comfort, reputation and will. He was fond of listing the forms it takes, and the list is uncomfortable reading because it catches almost everyone somewhere. Self-will, which must have its own way. Self-love, which cannot be neglected without pain. Self-confidence, which undertakes God’s work in its own strength. Self-consciousness, which is paralysed by what others think. Self-pity, which nurses its grievances. Self-seeking, self-defence, self-indulgence, self-justification. And most elusive of all, self-righteousness — the self admiring its own progress in crucifying itself.

And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. LUKE 9:23

Simpson pointed out that the Lord does not say deny yourself things. He says deny yourself — disown the self as the governing principle. The denial of things is easy by comparison, and can be performed with considerable self-satisfaction.

Not suppression, but exchange

Here Simpson parts company with mere asceticism, and the distinction is the heart of his teaching. You cannot remove the self by attacking it. Every attempt produces a new and subtler form of the same thing, because the one doing the attacking is the self. A man may starve his body, renounce his ambitions and cultivate a reputation for humility, and be more thoroughly self-occupied at the end than at the beginning. The remedy is not subtraction but substitution. The self life is displaced by the Christ life, as darkness is displaced by light rather than removed by effort.

He must increase, but I must decrease. JOHN 3:30

Simpson insisted on the order in that verse. The increase comes first, and the decrease follows from it. We do not diminish ourselves in order to make room for Christ; we receive Christ, and our own importance quietly collapses because something larger has arrived.

The daily cross

Note the word daily in Luke 9:23. Simpson took it seriously, and it guards his teaching against the misuse that has attended every doctrine of surrender. The reckoning of Romans 6 is settled once. Its application is renewed every morning, and generally in circumstances we did not choose. The cross is presented to us not as an abstraction but as an interruption, a slight, an inconvenience, a person who will not do what we want.

For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:11

The clause at the end is the point. The dying is never an end in itself. It is always in order that something else may appear.

Personality is not the enemy

A caution that Simpson supplied himself, and that his followers sometimes lost. The self life is not the same as personality, temperament or natural ability. God made those and intends to use them. The goal is not a colourless Christian — Simpson himself remained recognisably a driven, visionary, organising Scotsman to the end of his days, and the movement he built could not have existed otherwise. What goes to the cross is the self as centre, not the self as creature. Peter after Pentecost is still impetuous Peter; the impetuousness now serves Christ instead of Peter.

For to me to live is Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:21

There is a test in this that requires no theology to apply.

Watch what happens in you the next time you are contradicted, overlooked, or corrected in front of others. Whatever rises in that moment, unbidden, before you have time to arrange your face — that is the thing this chapter is about.

Self in the Lord’s work

The subtlest form of the self life, Simpson observed, does not appear in worldly pursuits at all. It appears in ministry, where it is nearly invisible because everything about it looks like devotion. Self can want a platform and call it a burden for souls. It can resent a colleague’s success and call it concern for sound doctrine. It can labour to exhaustion and call it consecration when the real engine is the need to be needed. It can defend its position tenaciously and call it contending for the faith. The New Testament knows this problem and names names.

I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.

Paul, remarkably, was able to distinguish between the message and the motive of those who preached it, and to rejoice even where the motive was bad.

Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife …What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice. PHILIPPIANS 1:15, 18

Simpson drew two things from this. First, that God is able to use a ministry in which self is heavily involved, which should relieve us of the anxiety that nothing will be blessed until our motives are pure — they never will be entirely. And second, that this must never become an excuse for leaving the motives unexamined. The practical test he suggested is uncomfortable and quick. How do you feel when someone else is used to do the thing you wanted to do? The answer arrives before you can arrange it, and it is generally accurate.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Go through Simpson’s list — self-will, self-pity, self-defence, self-seeking — and name the one that fits you most exactly. 2. Stop attacking the self directly. Give the same energy to receiving Christ, and watch what happens to the other.

3. Take the next contradiction or slight as the day’s cross rather than as an obstacle to your spiritual life. It is the material. 4. When you are misunderstood this week, decline to defend yourself once, and observe what rises. 5. Distinguish self from personality. Do not seek to be less yourself; seek to be less your own centre.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have been trimming branches for years, and the root is untouched.
I see it now: not merely my sins, but myself — at the centre, arranging everything, wanting my own way and calling it conviction.
I cannot crucify myself; every attempt has made me proud of the attempt. So come and increase, and let me decrease as a consequence rather than an achievement.
Give me today’s cross, and let me take it without complaint — that the life of Jesus might be seen in me. Amen.

fields.title: Wholly Sanctified
fields.body_html:
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:23

Simpson wrote a small book on this single verse, and the title he gave it is the word he would not let go of: Wholly Sanctified. The emphasis falls on the adverb. Paul does not pray that the Thessalonians be partly sanctified, or sanctified in their religious department. He prays for the whole person, and then names the parts in case anyone should misunderstand: spirit, and soul, and body.

What the word means

Simpson began where the Old Testament begins, because the vocabulary comes from there. To sanctify is to set apart. When the vessels of the tabernacle were sanctified they were not morally improved — a bowl has no morals. They were transferred from ordinary use to God’s use. That is the root idea, and it is the reason sanctification is not primarily about the removal of faults.

If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master’s use, and prepared unto every good work. 2 TIMOTHY 2:21

There are two movements in it, and Simpson insisted on both. There is separation from — the withdrawal of the vessel from common service. And there is consecration to — its dedication to the owner who will now use it as He pleases. A great deal of holiness teaching stops at the first, and produces Christians whose religion is chiefly a list of things they do not do. Separation without consecration yields an empty vessel, scrupulously clean and used for nothing. The point of taking the bowl off the common shelf is to put it on the altar.

Spirit, soul and body

Paul’s threefold naming gave Simpson his structure, and he applied it concretely. The spirit is sanctified when a man’s deepest life is turned Godward — when his communion, his conscience and his intuitive sense of God’s will are governed by the Holy Spirit rather than by his own preferences. The soul is sanctified when the mind, the emotions and the will come under Christ. Simpson gave particular attention to this middle region, because it is where most Christians live and where most of the trouble is. A sanctified mind is not merely a mind that thinks correct doctrine; it is one whose habitual imagination has been cleansed. Sanctified emotions are not suppressed emotions; they are affections attached to what deserves them. A sanctified will is not a broken will but a surrendered one.

And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. ROMANS 12:2

The body is sanctified when its members are placed at God’s disposal — the eyes, the tongue, the appetite, the hands, the hours. Simpson took this literally and unsentimentally, and it is the point at which his teaching on holiness runs directly into his teaching on healing: the body is not a regrettable container for the soul but a temple bought at a price.

What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you …ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body. 1 CORINTHIANS 6:19–20

The One who does it

Now the sentence that Simpson regarded as the whole security of the doctrine, and which is almost always left off when the verse is quoted.

Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:24

Paul does not command the Thessalonians to sanctify themselves wholly. He prays that God will do it, and then adds that God is faithful and will. This is the guard against the two diseases of holiness teaching. It prevents despair, because the outcome does not rest on the believer’s capacity. And it prevents pride, because a work God performs leaves nobody anything to boast about. Simpson’s counsel was accordingly simple. Present the vessel; God will fill and use it. Our part is the handing over; His part is everything that follows.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

Wholly, and therefore now

One further observation, and it is the practical sting of the chapter. The word wholly exposes the arrangement most of us actually operate. We have consecrated regions. There is a part of life we have handed over — usually the explicitly religious part — and there are territories that have never come up in prayer at all: how money is spent, how a spouse is spoken to, what is watched alone, what is done with anger, how a business treats those who cannot complain. Simpson’s question was not whether you have surrendered, but whether there is anything you have quietly kept off the list. And he noticed that most believers can name it within a few seconds of being asked, which suggests they have known about it for some time.

There is a mercy hidden in the word preserved in this verse, which Simpson pointed out and which is easily missed. Paul does not merely ask that the Thessalonians be sanctified; he asks that they be preserved blameless until the coming of Christ. The One who sets the vessel apart also keeps it. That is a longer commitment than any of us would make about ourselves, and it is offered by Someone who does not tire.

Keeping the surrender

A consecration once made does not stay made without attention, and Simpson was realistic about the leakage. The New Testament image he used was the altar. The sacrifice is laid on it in a definite act — but Paul’s phrase is a living sacrifice, and a living sacrifice can get down. Nothing holds it there but its own continuing consent.

If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. LUKE 9:23

Daily. The word is in the text, and Simpson would not let it be softened into a general disposition. The handing over is renewed each morning, usually before anything has happened to make it feel necessary. He recommended a specific practice, and it is worth adopting because it takes about ninety seconds. On waking, before the day’s demands arrive, present the day: the hours, the people, the interruptions not yet known, the temper not yet tested. Not a long devotion — a definite transfer of ownership, made in words, before the ownership is contested.

O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee. PSALM 63:1

The reason for doing this early is practical. By ten o’clock the day has taken shape, several small decisions have been made on autopilot, and the surrender is now being attempted against resistance rather than in advance of it. Simpson’s observation was that most believers who lose ground do not lose it in a crisis. They lose it in the accumulation of mornings on which the transfer was simply not made.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the territory you have never brought into prayer. You will know it immediately. Bring it now. 2. Check whether your holiness is chiefly separation from things. If the vessel is clean and unused, that is only half the doctrine. 3. Take Paul’s three areas in turn and name one specific thing in each — spirit, soul, body — that needs to be handed over. 4. Rest on 1 Thessalonians 5:24. Where you have despaired of change, remind God of His own promise to do it. 5. Present the vessel again this morning, and then get on with the day instead of monitoring yourself.

A PRAYER
God of peace, sanctify me wholly — not the religious part, not the part that shows, but all of it.
Take my spirit, and make my communion with You real. Take my soul — my mind with its wandering, my feelings with their disorder, my will with its insistence. Take my body, my eyes and tongue and appetite and hours.
There is one place I have kept back, and You know what it is. I bring it now.
Faithful is He who calls me, who also will do it. I rest on that, because I have proved I cannot do it myself. Amen.

fields.title: The Land of Promise
fields.body_html:
So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief. HEBREWS 3:19

Simpson’s favourite way of describing the Christian life was a map, and the map came from the book of Joshua. Israel’s history divides into three: Egypt, the wilderness, and Canaan. And he held — following a reading with a long pedigree in Puritan and Keswick teaching — that these correspond to three conditions in which people may be found.

Three places

Egypt is bondage. A person in Egypt is not God’s, has not been redeemed, and is a slave whether or not he knows it. The wilderness is the condition Simpson was most concerned about. Here are people who have genuinely left Egypt — the blood has been applied, the sea has been crossed, they belong to God — and who are going in circles. They are saved and defeated. They have real experience of God’s provision and no possession of anything. They live on manna, complain a good deal, and remember Egypt with a fondness that horrifies them. Canaan is the land of promise: not comfort, but possession. Now the crucial point, and Simpson made it repeatedly because the mistake is so common. Canaan is not heaven. We sing about crossing Jordan as a figure for dying, and it makes for good hymns, but it will not survive examination. There are giants in Canaan. There are walled cities, unconquered territory, defeats like Ai, and forty years of warfare. Nobody fights battles in heaven. Canaan is a picture of the Christian life as God intends it now — a life of rest and conflict at once, in which the believer possesses what has been given him and has to take ground to do it.

Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you. JOSHUA 1:3

Note the tense. Have I given. The land is already theirs by grant; they enter into what is already legally theirs.

Why a generation did not enter

The wilderness generation stood at the border at Kadesh-barnea and did not go in. Simpson dwelt on the reason, because Scripture states it plainly and it is not what we would guess. They did not fail through weakness, or through sin in the ordinary sense, or because the giants were genuinely too large. They failed through unbelief. Ten of the twelve spies reported accurately about the giants and inaccurately about God.

And they brought up an evil report of the land …and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight. NUMBERS 13:32–33
So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief. HEBREWS 3:19

The writer to the Hebrews applies this directly to Christians, which is what licenses the whole comparison. He is not making a devotional analogy; he is arguing that the same danger stands over the church.

There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God …Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief. HEBREWS 4:9, 11

Crossing Jordan

Between the wilderness and the land lies a river, and Simpson made much of the manner of the crossing. The Red Sea is deliverance from Egypt — redemption, the picture of the cross applied to our guilt. Jordan is different. Seated, and wrestling — in the same letter, to the same people. Simpson took that as the exact description of Canaan: the ground is given, and it must still be taken. You have given me the land. Teach me to put my foot on it.
Take me across Jordan — through the death and resurrection of Your Son — into what You have already granted, and let me stop living on emergency rations in sight of Your abundance. Amen.

fields.title: The Indwelling Spirit
fields.body_html:
Even the Spirit of truth …for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. JOHN 14:17

Simpson wrote more on the Holy Spirit than on any other subject except Christ Himself, and his treatment has a particular character that distinguishes it from much that has been written since.

A Person, not a power

His first insistence was elementary and constantly neglected: the Holy Spirit is a Person. The pronouns in the upper room discourse are personal — he, not it — and the activities ascribed to Him are the activities of a person. He teaches, guides, reminds, convinces, forbids, appoints, intercedes. He can be grieved, which no force can be. He can be lied to, resisted and quenched.

And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. EPHESIANS 4:30

Simpson pressed the practical consequence hard. If the Spirit is a power, the question is how to get more of Him and how to use Him. If He is a Person, those questions are impertinent. You do not use a person. The question becomes how not to grieve Him, and how much of you He has. He put it in a form that has been repeated ever since: the issue is not whether you have the Holy Spirit but whether the Holy Spirit has you.

With you, and in you

The verse at the head of this chapter contains a distinction that Simpson regarded as the hinge of the whole subject. He dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. Before Pentecost the Spirit was with the disciples — accompanying, empowering, working alongside. After Pentecost He would be in them. That change is the great privilege of the present age. The Old Testament records the Spirit coming upon particular people for particular tasks and departing again. The New Testament describes something unprecedented: permanent residence in ordinary believers.

Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? 1 CORINTHIANS 3:16
Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. ROMANS 8:9

Simpson was careful with that last verse, because it settles a question people still get wrong. The indwelling Spirit is not the possession of an advanced class of Christian. Every believer has Him; nobody is a believer without Him. Whatever the fullness of the Spirit means — and the next chapter takes that up — it cannot mean receiving a Spirit one previously lacked.

His work is to glorify Christ

Here is the feature that most distinguishes Simpson’s teaching, and it is the best safeguard against the excesses that have attended this doctrine.

He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you. JOHN 16:14

The Holy Spirit’s stated purpose is not to draw attention to Himself. It is to make Christ real. He is, as Simpson liked to say, the executive of the Godhead in this age, whose whole business is to take what belongs to Jesus and make it actual in believers. This yields a test that can be applied to any teaching, meeting or movement claiming the Spirit’s authority. Does it leave people occupied with the Spirit and His manifestations, or occupied with Christ? A ministry genuinely full of the Holy Spirit will tend to talk about Jesus, because that is what the Spirit does. It also explains why Simpson’s Fourfold Gospel has no separate wheel for the Holy Spirit, which puzzles some readers. It is not an omission. In his thinking the Spirit is the one who administers all four — the agent by whom Christ is Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King within us.

The Spirit and the ordinary

One further note, because Simpson’s own life illustrates it. We associate the Spirit’s work with the extraordinary, and Scripture does record extraordinary things. But the great bulk of what the New Testament attributes to Him is unspectacular: assurance that we are God’s children, help in prayer when we do not know what to ask, the slow production of character, the ability to call God Father and mean it.

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. ROMANS 8:16
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought. ROMANS 8:26

A believer who has never had a dramatic experience and who prays, endures, loves awkward people and grows slowly kinder is exhibiting the work of the Holy Spirit as certainly as anyone.

The question to carry out of this chapter is not how to obtain more of the Spirit. It is how much of you He has, and where you have been grieving Him — a question a Person can be asked directly.

How He leads

If the Spirit indwells the believer, how does His guidance actually arrive? Simpson’s answer was deliberately unspectacular.

For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God. ROMANS 8:14

He identified several ordinary means, and insisted they normally agree. The Word, which is the primary and governing means. Most of what God wants from a believer on any given day is already written, and no further guidance is required to begin obeying it. The inward witness — a settled sense of peace about a course, or an inward check against it. Simpson took this seriously without making it decisive on its own.

And let the peace of God rule in your hearts. COLOSSIANS 3:15

Circumstances, which God arranges, and counsel, which He supplies through mature believers who know us and are not impressed by us. His rule of thumb was that these ordinarily converge, and that a believer should be slow to act on one against the others. An impression that contradicts Scripture is not the Spirit, whatever it feels like. An open door that requires disobedience is not from God, however convenient. He was equally firm about the danger. Believers who elevate impressions to the level of revelation become unteachable, since any objection can be answered by appeal to a private message no one else can examine. Simpson had watched this wreck people, and he never allowed the inward sense to be treated as an authority in its own right. The Spirit who speaks within is the same Spirit who wrote the Word, and He does not contradict Himself.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Stop asking for more of the Spirit and start asking what part of you He does not yet have. 2. Identify one thing you know grieves Him. Deal with that before seeking any further experience. 3. Apply the John 16:14 test to whatever teaching you are under: does it leave you occupied with Christ? 4. Thank God for the unspectacular evidences — assurance, help in prayer, slow growth in kindness. These are His work. 5. Speak to the Spirit as a Person this week, not as a resource.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, I have treated You as a power to be obtained rather than a Person to be obeyed. Forgive me.
You dwell in me. I do not need to fetch You from a distance or persuade You to come. The question is how much of me You have, and I think we both know the answer.
Show me where I am grieving You, and give me no rest about it.
And do in me what You came to do: take the things of Christ and make them real, until I am occupied with Him and not with my own experience. Amen.
