fields.title: Filled with the Spirit
fields.body_html:
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit. EPHESIANS 5:18

If every believer has the Holy Spirit, what is the fullness, and why does Paul have to command it? Simpson’s answer began with the grammar. The verb in Ephesians 5:18 is an imperative, which means the fullness is not automatic; and it is continuous, which means it is not a single event to be obtained and filed away. Paul is commanding a state to be maintained.

Full of what is already there

His illustration was the difference between a vessel that contains water and one that is full of it. Every believer has the Spirit; the question is displacement. A jar with an inch of water in it and a great deal of air is not empty — but it is not full either. The filling of the Spirit is not the arrival of more Spirit from outside. It is the Spirit occupying more of the person. This explains the terms of the contrast Paul chose. A man under the influence of drink is controlled by it: his speech, his judgment and his behaviour are governed by something other than himself. Paul’s point is not about the pleasure but about the control. To be filled with the Spirit is to be under His government at that level.

And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness. ACTS 4:31

Simpson noted that the people filled in Acts 4 include several who had already been filled in Acts 2. The fullness is repeatable, which is fatal to any scheme that treats it as a once-for-all attainment.

The conditions

Simpson set out what a believer may do, and was careful that none of it becomes a technique for extracting something from God. Emptying. A vessel already full of something else cannot be filled. The practical work here is honest inventory: what occupies the space — ambition, resentment, a hidden appetite, self-pity? Asking. The promise is explicit and the terms are generous.

If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13

Obeying. The Spirit is given to the obedient, not to the impressive.

And so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him. ACTS 5:32

Taking by faith. Here Simpson applied his general principle: what God promises is received by faith, not produced by feeling. A believer who has emptied, asked and obeyed may take the fullness on the strength of the promise and go about his business, whether or not anything registers emotionally.

The question of tongues

This chapter cannot avoid the controversy that broke over Simpson’s movement after 1906, and his handling of it is one of the more instructive episodes in his life. The Pentecostal revival spread rapidly through the constituencies nearest to his own, and many Alliance people were caught up in it. The question pressed on him was whether speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence that a believer has been baptised or filled with the Spirit. Simpson did not answer from the sidelines. He wanted everything God had. In August 1907 he returned to the same pine woods at Old Orchard where he had been healed, and asked God for a fuller baptism of the Spirit with all His gifts and graces. He did not speak in tongues, then or afterwards. His conclusion was threefold. Tongues is a genuine gift of the Spirit, not to be despised or forbidden. It is not the necessary evidence of the Spirit’s fullness, since Scripture nowhere makes it the test and Paul asks plainly whether all speak with tongues, expecting the answer no (1 Corinthians 12:30). And believers should not make it the object of pursuit, because the Spirit distributes gifts as He wills rather than as we select.

But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:11

The policy he settled on has marked his movement ever since, and it is expressed in four words: seek not, forbid not. It cost him. He lost people who wanted more and people who wanted the door closed. Christians still divide over this, and readers of this book will hold different views. What is worth learning from Simpson is not necessarily his conclusion but his method: he examined the Scriptures, sought God about it personally at real cost, refused to despise believers whose experience differed from his own, and declined to make a secondary matter into a test of spirituality.

The evidence that is not disputed

Whatever one concludes about the gifts, Scripture is not ambiguous about what the Spirit’s fullness produces.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance. GALATIANS 5:22–23
But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me. ACTS 1:8

Character and witness. Simpson’s rule of thumb was that a man filled with the Spirit becomes more like Christ and more useful to Christ, and that any claimed fullness which produces neither should be examined rather than celebrated.

The most practical thing in this chapter is the inventory. Before asking for more, find out what is occupying the room.

Power for what

A question worth asking of the whole subject: what is the fullness for? The promise in Acts answers it, and the answer is narrower than we sometimes assume.

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. ACTS 1:8

The power is given for witness. Not for personal exhilaration, not for a sense of spiritual arrival, and not for standing among other Christians. It is equipment for a task, and the task is other people. Simpson pressed this hard, because he had watched the deeper life become, in some hands, an elaborate form of self-cultivation — believers pursuing ever richer inward experiences while the city outside remained unevangelised and the poor remained unvisited. The test he applied is simple. Has this fullness made you more useful to anybody?

The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:7

To profit withal — for the common good. Every genuine work of the Spirit in an individual is intended to arrive somewhere else. There is a mercy in this framing. A believer anxious about whether he has been filled can stop examining his sensations and ask a more answerable question: since last year, has anyone been helped through me who would not otherwise have been?

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Take an honest inventory of what fills you. Name one thing displacing the Spirit and deal with it before asking for anything. 2. Ask plainly, on the strength of Luke 11:13, and then act as though God has answered rather than waiting for a sensation. 3. Test any claimed fullness — your own included — by Galatians 5:22 and Acts 1:8. Character and witness. 4. Where you differ from other Christians about the gifts, adopt Simpson’s posture: study honestly, seek God personally, refuse contempt. 5. Renew the filling daily. It is a continuous command, not a certificate.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, I have asked for more of You when the problem was how much of me was already occupied.
Show me what fills the room. Empty me of the ambition, the grudge, the appetite, the self-pity that leaves so little space.
I ask, because my Father has promised to give You to those who ask. I take You at Your word, whether or not I feel anything.
Make me more like Christ and more useful to Him. Let those be the evidences, and let me not despise any believer whose experience differs from mine. Amen.

The filling of the Spirit is not the arrival of more Spirit from outside. It is the Spirit occupying more of the person. This explains the terms of the contrast Paul chose. A man under the influence of drink is controlled by it: his speech, his judgment and his behaviour are governed by something other than himself. Paul’s point is not about the pleasure but about the control. To be filled with the Spirit is to be under His government at that level. And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness. The fullness is repeatable, which is fatal to any scheme that treats it as a once-for-all attainment. The conditions Simpson set out what a believer may do, and was careful that none of it becomes a technique for extracting something from God. Emptying. A vessel already full of something else cannot be filled. The practical work here is honest inventory: what occupies the space — ambition, resentment, a hidden appetite, self-pity? Asking. The promise is explicit and the terms are generous. If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13 Obeying. The Spirit is given to the obedient, not to the impressive. And so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him. ACTS 5:32 Taking by faith. Here Simpson applied his general principle: what God promises is received by faith, not produced by feeling. A believer who has emptied, asked and obeyed may take the fullness on the strength of the promise and go about his business, whether or not anything registers emotionally. The question of tongues This chapter cannot avoid the controversy that broke over Simpson’s movement after 1906, and his handling of it is one of the more instructive episodes in his life. The Pentecostal revival spread rapidly through the constituencies nearest to his own, and many Alliance people were caught up in it. The question pressed on him was whether speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence that a believer has been baptised or filled with the Spirit. Simpson did not answer from the sidelines. He wanted everything God had. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance. Simpson’s rule of thumb was that a man filled with the Spirit becomes more like Christ and more useful to Christ, and that any claimed fullness which produces neither should be examined rather than celebrated. The most practical thing in this chapter is the inventory. Before asking for more, find out what is occupying the room. Power for what A question worth asking of the whole subject: what is the fullness for? The promise in Acts answers it, and the answer is narrower than we sometimes assume. But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. ACTS 1:8 The power is given for witness. Not for personal exhilaration, not for a sense of spiritual arrival, and not for standing among other Christians. It is equipment for a task, and the task is other people. Simpson pressed this hard, because he had watched the deeper life become, in some hands, an elaborate form of self-cultivation — believers pursuing ever richer inward experiences while the city outside remained unevangelised and the poor remained unvisited. The test he applied is simple. Has this fullness made you more useful to anybody? The manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:7 To profit withal — for the common good. Every genuine work of the Spirit in an individual is intended to arrive somewhere else. There is a mercy in this framing. A believer anxious about whether he has been filled can stop examining his sensations and ask a more answerable question: since last year, has anyone been helped through me who would not otherwise have been? FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Take an honest inventory of what fills you. Name one thing displacing the Spirit and deal with it before asking for anything. 2. Ask plainly, on the strength of Luke 11:13, and then act as though God has answered rather than waiting for a sensation. 3. Test any claimed fullness — your own included — by Galatians 5:22 and Acts 1:8. Character and witness. 4. Where you differ from other Christians about the gifts, adopt Simpson’s posture: study honestly, seek God personally, refuse contempt. 5. Renew the filling daily. It is a continuous command, not a certificate. A PRAYER Holy Spirit, I have asked for more of You when the problem was how much of me was already occupied. Show me what fills the room. Empty me of the ambition, the grudge, the appetite, the self-pity that leaves so little space. I ask, because my Father has promised to give You to those who ask. I take You at Your word, whether or not I feel anything. Make me more like Christ and more useful to Him. Let those be the evidences, and let me not despise any believer whose experience differs from mine. Amen.

fields.title: A Larger Christian Life
fields.body_html:
Enlarge the place of thy tent …spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes. ISAIAH 54:2

Simpson gave one of his books the title A Larger Christian Life, and the phrase captures a conviction that runs through everything he did: that most believers are living in a smaller world than God has provided, and that the limitation is entirely on our side.

Straitened in ourselves

His controlling text was a remark of Paul’s to a difficult congregation.

O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged. Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:11–12

Straitened means narrowed, cramped, confined. Paul tells them that whatever constriction they feel in the relationship is not coming from his end. He is wide open. The narrowness is theirs. Simpson applied this to our dealings with God, and the application is uncomfortable. When our Christian life feels small — when God seems distant, prayer feels mechanical, and the supply appears inadequate — our instinct is to conclude that heaven is being sparing. The apostle’s diagnosis points the other way. The pipe is not narrow at the source.

I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it. PSALM 81:10

That is an extraordinary invitation, and Simpson observed that most of us respond to it with a very modest request and then complain about the size of the answer.

Three enlargements

He worked the theme out in several directions, and three are worth naming. Larger views of God. Almost every spiritual problem, Simpson thought, traces back to a God who has been mentally reduced — made manageable, predictable, and roughly the size of our own experience. The remedy is not technique but sight.

Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us. EPHESIANS 3:20

Note where Paul sets the ceiling: not at what we ask, which would be generous, but above what we can even conceive of asking. Any request we bring is therefore beneath the limit by definition. Larger faith. Simpson observed that we tend to ask God for what we can already imagine arranging ourselves, with a small margin added for divine assistance. He urged believers to ask for things that would be embarrassing if God did not act — and then to be willing to wait. Larger service. His own life is the argument. He had a comfortable pulpit and gave it up to work among people who could not pay him, and the result was a movement on several continents. He held that most Christians are prevented from any significant usefulness not by lack of gifting but by the smallness of what they have offered.

Enlargement is not always comfortable

The honest half of the chapter, which Simpson did not hide. The verse in Isaiah tells the tent-dweller to lengthen the cords and strengthen the stakes. A larger tent needs deeper anchoring, or the first storm takes it. Enlargement of capacity is generally accompanied by enlargement of pressure, and God rarely gives one without the other. Simpson’s own enlargements came through a nervous collapse, a heart condition, a resignation that cost him his income and his denomination, the burial of children, and the loss of friends on both sides of a controversy he did not start. He was not describing an easier life. He was describing a bigger one.

Thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress. PSALM 4:1

That is the honest order in most lives. The distress comes first, and the enlargement is what God does with it.

There is a diagnostic worth applying. Look at what you asked God for this month. Would any of it have required Him to act? Or could most of it have happened through ordinary competence and reasonable luck? The answer tells you the size of the tent you are living in, and it is not a verdict on God’s supply.

Enlarged towards people

The enlargement Simpson pressed hardest was not in faith or service but in affection, because it is the one we are least willing to attempt.

And the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men. 1 THESSALONIANS 3:12

Paul’s prayer has two directions, and the second is the difficult one. One toward another covers the people we already like. Toward all men does not. Simpson observed that most Christians have a heart of a fixed size, into which a certain number of people fit, and that we manage the limit by quietly excluding those who are difficult, tedious, foreign, poor, or who have wronged us. The exclusions are never announced; they are simply operated. His prescription was not to feel differently, which nobody can produce on demand, but to act deliberately in the direction of the enlargement and let the affection follow. Speak to the person you have been avoiding. Give to someone who cannot reciprocate. Take an interest in a country you have never thought about.

Now for a recompence in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:13

There is a connection here with everything else in the chapter that is easy to miss. A cramped heart towards people generally accompanies a cramped view of God, because our sense of how much we have received governs how freely we give. The person who believes he has been forgiven a great deal finds it strangely easy to be generous, and the person who believes he was not that bad to begin with finds it strangely hard.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Review your recent prayers. How many required God to do something you could not arrange? 2. Ask for one thing this month that would be plainly embarrassing if God did not act. Then wait without withdrawing the request. 3. Identify where you have concluded that God is being sparing. Consider Paul’s diagnosis instead: the narrowness may be at your end. 4. Offer something larger — more time, more money, a willingness you have been withholding — and see what God does with it. 5. Strengthen the stakes as well as lengthening the cords. Deepen a discipline before you seek a wider ministry.

A PRAYER
Father, I have lived in a small tent and blamed the weather.
You are able to do exceeding abundantly above all that I ask or think, and my asking has been careful, modest and mostly within reach of my own competence. Forgive the smallness of it.
Enlarge me — my view of You, my expectation, my service, my heart towards people I find difficult.
And when the enlargement comes through distress, as it usually does, hold me steady. Lengthen my cords, but strengthen my stakes. Amen.

fields.title: The Life of Faith
fields.body_html:
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. HEBREWS 11:1

Everything in Simpson’s teaching is received the same way, and it is worth setting out how he understood the receiving.

Faith is a definite act

His characteristic emphasis was that faith is not a mood but a transaction — something a believer does at a particular moment, on the strength of something God has said. His own healing is the pattern. He did not drift into a general confidence about his health. He went into the woods, settled the scriptural question, and made a definite pledge: taking Christ then and there as the life of his body. He wrote it down. He dated it. Afterwards, when symptoms returned, he did not renegotiate — he referred back to a transaction already completed.

He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; and being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. ROMANS 4:20–21

Simpson urged believers to make such transactions explicitly rather than hoping vaguely. A vague faith cannot be tested, cannot be remembered, and cannot be stood upon when feelings change — which they will.

Faith rests on a word, not on itself

The distinction that keeps this from becoming dangerous is where faith is placed. Faith is not a force we generate, and its power does not lie in its intensity. It lies entirely in its object. A weak grip on a strong rope is safer than a fierce grip on nothing.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

Which means the way to increase faith is not to try to believe harder. It is to find out what God has actually said, since faith is produced by the Word rather than by effort. Simpson’s counsel to the struggling was always to send them back to a specific promise rather than to exhort them to greater conviction. He also distinguished sharply between faith and presumption. Faith takes hold of something God has promised. Presumption takes hold of something we want and attaches God’s name to it. The difference is not the strength of the confidence — presumption is often more confident — but whether there is a word from God underneath.

And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us. 1 JOHN 5:14

Faith and feeling

Simpson returned constantly to the order of these two, because reversing them had wrecked so many. The natural sequence we want is: feel, then believe. God’s sequence is: believe, and the feeling follows or does not, and either way the fact stands. His own conversion was the first lesson in this. He took Christ at fifteen with no emotion whatever and spent some time troubled by the absence, until he understood that he had been looking for evidence in the wrong place. He built the rest of his life on that order.

For we walk by faith, not by sight. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:7

An honest caution

Teaching of this kind has a shadow, and it must be named. When faith is presented as the decisive factor, a believer whose prayer is not answered can only conclude that his faith was insufficient — and from there it is a short step to a religion of anxious self-examination, and a shorter one to telling the suffering that their trouble is their own fault. Simpson himself was more careful than some of his followers, but the danger is real and this book has already met it in chapter four. Three guards are necessary. Faith is God’s gift, not our achievement — it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). Its measure is not a moral score. Unanswered prayer is not proof of unbelief. Paul asked three times and was refused, and no one has ever suggested his faith was defective. And the object of faith is a Person with His own wisdom, not a mechanism that delivers on demand. The father in Mark 9 who said he believed and asked for help with his unbelief received exactly what he asked for, which suggests that God’s threshold is lower than ours.

Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. MARK 9:24

Faith, then, is neither a feeling nor a force. It is taking God at His word, in a definite act, about a specific thing He has actually said — and then behaving as though it were true, because it is.

Faith puts its foot in the water

Faith, in Scripture, characteristically acts before it sees — and Simpson’s favourite illustration was the crossing of Jordan. The river was in flood. The instruction given to the priests carrying the ark was that they should step into the water, and that the waters would then be cut off.

And it shall come to pass, as soon as the soles of the feet of the priests …shall rest in the waters of Jordan …the waters of Jordan shall be cut off. JOSHUA 3:13

The order is unmistakable. The feet go in first; the river parts afterwards. Had the priests waited for evidence that the promise was reliable, they would have stood on the bank for the rest of their lives. Simpson applied this to the sticking point in most Christian experience. We wait for the assurance before we act, and God has arranged matters so that the assurance arrives in the acting.

Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. JAMES 2:18

James is not correcting Paul. He is describing the same faith from the outside. What cannot be seen directly can be inferred from what a person actually does, and a faith that never issues in an act cannot be distinguished from an opinion. The practical counsel is uncomfortable and short. Identify the step you have been waiting to feel ready for. Note that you have been waiting a considerable time. Take it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Find a specific promise of God that covers your present need. Not a general impression — a text. 2. Make a definite transaction about it: put it in words, write the date, and tell God you are taking Him at His word. 3. When feelings contradict it later, do not renegotiate. Refer back. 4. Test whether you are exercising faith or presumption. Is there a word from God underneath, or only something you want?

5. If your faith feels small, pray Mark 9:24 exactly as it stands. It was answered.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have called it faith when it was only hoping, and I have wondered why nothing was settled.
Show me what You have actually promised. Let my confidence rest on Your word and not on the strength of my own believing.
I take You at Your word today about the thing I have brought You. When my feelings say otherwise, hold me to what was settled.
And where my faith is small, I say what the father said: I believe; help my unbelief. You did not turn him away. Amen.

fields.title: The Life of Prayer
fields.body_html:
Men ought always to pray, and not to faint. LUKE 18:1

Simpson built a movement, a college, a magazine and a missionary society, and he maintained throughout that none of it was the real work. The real work was prayer, and everything visible was the overflow.

Communion before petition

His first insistence was that prayer is fellowship before it is request. We generally reverse this. Prayer, for most of us, is the department of the Christian life where we bring needs, and its health is measured by whether the needs are met. On that basis a season of unanswered prayer feels like a failed relationship, because the relationship was constructed entirely around transactions. Simpson taught believers to begin by attending to God Himself — which is simply chapter one applied to the prayer closet. Petition follows, and belongs there, but it is not the foundation.

But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret. MATTHEW 6:6

The instruction is about a Person and a door, not a list.

Abiding prayer

His governing text for the whole subject came from the vine discourse, and he would not let the first clause be detached from the second.

If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you. JOHN 15:7

The promise at the end is breathtaking, and it is conditioned twice. The one who abides in Christ, and in whom Christ’s words abide, will find his asking answered — because such a person’s wants have been progressively reshaped. He is not receiving a blank cheque; he has become someone who wants what God wants. Simpson drew from this that the way to improve one’s prayer life is largely indirect. Time spent in the Word alters what one asks for, and the alteration does more for the answered-prayer rate than any refinement of technique.

Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. JAMES 4:3

Asking, and taking

Here is a distinction characteristic of Simpson, and it follows from the last chapter. He distinguished between the prayer of supplication — asking, and continuing to ask, for something not yet given — and the prayer of faith, in which the believer, having found a promise and become settled, takes what God has offered and moves from petition to thanksgiving.

Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them. MARK 11:24

Note the tense. Believe that ye receive — at the point of asking, before anything is visible. Simpson was careful to keep both kinds. He did not teach that persistent asking is a sign of weak faith; the Lord’s own parables commend the widow who would not stop. But he held that there comes a point, on some matters, when the believer has heard from God and may stop asking and start thanking — and that many Christians never arrive there because they have never settled what God has actually said.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. PHILIPPIANS 4:6

With thanksgiving — before the answer, not after it.

Simpson connected prayer directly to the indwelling Spirit, and this rescued the subject from being a matter of human exertion.

Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us. ROMANS 8:26

The admission in that verse — we know not what we should pray for — was, in Simpson’s view, one of the most liberating in Scripture. We are not required to diagnose situations correctly before we may pray about them. The Spirit within supplies what we lack, including the content. He regarded that as an invitation extended to the church, and he took it literally.

The most useful practical counsel he gave about prayer was also the least inspiring: keep an appointment. Feeling will not sustain it. A fixed time, kept whether or not anything is felt, outlasts every burst of enthusiasm — and it is generally in the unfelt sessions that the real work is done.

Simpson gave attention to the question every praying person eventually asks: when prayer seems to meet a ceiling, is there anything to look for? The word is regard — not commit, but harbour and protect. The issue is not failure but tolerance. Unforgiveness. The Lord attached this directly to prayer, in a passage about mountains being moved.

Some delays are the exercise of faith, and some are simply the wisdom of God, who occasionally answers no. The list is for personal examination, and it should be worked through honestly and then left alone.

1. Begin your next prayer time with ten minutes that contain no requests at all. 2. Fix an appointment and keep it on the days you do not feel like it, especially those. 3. Take one matter you have been asking about for months. Find what God has said about it, and consider whether it is time to move from asking to thanking. 4. Pray for one country and one worker by name this week. Keep it up for a month. 5. When you do not know how to pray about something, say so, and ask the Spirit to supply what you lack.

A PRAYER
Father, I have treated prayer as a place to bring needs, and when the needs were unmet I concluded that something had failed.
Teach me to come for You before I come for anything.
Let Your words abide in me until what I ask for has quietly changed. Where you have spoken, give me the boldness to stop asking and begin thanking.
And when I do not know what to pray, pray in me by Your Spirit — for people I have forgotten, and for nations I will never see. Amen.

fields.title: Christ in All the Scriptures
fields.body_html:
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. LUKE 24:27

Simpson’s largest literary undertaking was a commentary on the whole Bible, and its title states his method: Christ in the Bible. He worked through book after book asking one question of each — where is Christ here?

The Lord’s own method

He took his warrant from the road to Emmaus. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem in complete confusion, and the risen Christ, unrecognised, gives them a Bible study. He does not begin with the resurrection appearances. He begins at Moses, works through the prophets, and shows them the things concerning Himself in all the Scriptures.

And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you …that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. LUKE 24:44

Simpson pointed out that this covers the entire Hebrew canon in its three divisions. The claim is not that the Old Testament contains a few messianic predictions. It is that the whole thing is about Him.

Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. JOHN 5:39
Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me. HEBREWS 10:7

Types and shadows

Simpson’s practice was to look for Christ in three ways. In prophecy — the direct predictions, from the seed of the woman in Genesis 3 to the messenger of the covenant at the close of Malachi. In type — persons, institutions and events that prefigure Him. The New Testament does this itself and thereby licenses the method: Adam is called a figure of Him that was to come; Melchizedek is expounded at length in Hebrews; the passover lamb, the brazen serpent, the rock in the wilderness, the sacrifices and the tabernacle are all applied to Christ by New Testament writers.

For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us. 1 CORINTHIANS 5:7

And in the names and titles — a study Simpson loved. He wrote a whole book on the names of Jesus, holding that each reveals a distinct relation in which He meets a distinct need.

Why this matters practically

Three consequences, and Simpson pressed all of them. It unifies the Bible. Many believers experience Scripture as two disconnected books, and quietly abandon most of the first. If Christ is the subject throughout, the whole becomes coherent. It keeps the Old Testament from moralism. Read without Christ, the narratives become a gallery of examples: be brave like David, be pure like Joseph, be patient like Job. Simpson regarded that as a subtle return to salvation by imitation. The stories are not primarily about how to behave; they point to One who did what none of the characters could. And it feeds devotion. A believer who has learned to look for Christ in every passage will not run dry, because the subject is inexhaustible.

That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings. PHILIPPIANS 3:10

The necessary caution

Honesty requires a warning, because this method has a well-known failure mode and Simpson does not always avoid it. Typology can be pressed until every detail becomes a symbol and the interpreter is no longer reading the text but decorating it. Once the discipline goes, a man can find whatever he brought with him, and the Bible ceases to be able to correct him — which is precisely the opposite of what Scripture is for. The safeguards are straightforward. Follow the New Testament’s own examples rather than inventing new ones. Establish what a passage meant in its own setting before asking what it foreshadows; the two are not rivals, but the order matters. Hold typological readings as illumination rather than doctrine, and never build a teaching on a shadow that is not stated plainly somewhere in the light. Applied with those, the method is one of the great gifts of the older expositors, and it has largely been lost.

Try it once and the appeal becomes obvious. Take a passage you find dull — Leviticus, a genealogy, a chapter of Kings — and ask the Emmaus question: where is Christ here? You will not always find a clean answer. You will not read that chapter the same way again.

The names of God

One of Simpson’s favourite exercises was tracing the compound names of God through the Old Testament, and reading each as a disclosure of what Christ would prove to be. Where Abraham found a ram caught in a thicket, the place was named for the God who provides.

And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the Lord it shall be seen. GENESIS 22:14

The bitter water at Marah was healed, and God revealed Himself there as the One who heals (Exodus 15:26). After the victory over Amalek, Moses built an altar and called it the Lord my banner (Exodus 17:15). Gideon, terrified, was met by the Lord send peace (Judges 6:24). The shepherd psalm opens with the Lord is my shepherd, and Ezekiel closes with a city whose name means the Lord is there. Simpson’s method was to place each beside a corresponding claim of Christ. The God who provides; and my God shall supply all your need (Philippians 4:19). The God who heals; and the One who went about healing. The banner; and thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory (1 Corinthians 15:57). The peace; and he is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). The shepherd; and I am the good shepherd (John 10:11). The Lord who is there; and lo, I am with you alway. The value of the exercise is not scholarly but devotional. It supplies a vocabulary for bringing a specific need to a specific aspect of Christ, and it demonstrates the continuity Simpson was always insisting upon: that the God who met His people at Marah and Peniel and Bethlehem is the same, and has not changed His character between the Testaments.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Luke 24:13–32 and notice what the risen Christ chose to do with two confused disciples. 2. Take one Old Testament passage this week and ask where Christ is in it. Write down what you find. 3. Check your Old Testament reading for moralism. Are you mostly extracting examples to imitate?

4. Study one name or title of Christ — Shepherd, Advocate, Bread, Rock — and trace it across both Testaments. 5. Keep the guard-rails: follow the New Testament’s own typology, and never build doctrine on a shadow alone.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You walked with two disconsolate men and opened the Scriptures until their hearts burned, and the subject was Yourself.
I have read large parts of Your Word as history, or as a set of examples to copy, and missed You in them.
Open the Scriptures to me. Let me find You in the law and the prophets and the psalms, in the sacrifices and the shadows and the names.
And keep me sober. Let me not find what I brought with me; let me find You. Amen.

fields.title: Days of Heaven upon Earth
fields.body_html:
That your days may be multiplied …as the days of heaven upon the earth. DEUTERONOMY 11:21

Simpson’s daily devotional, still in print more than a century later, takes its title from a phrase in Deuteronomy: days of heaven upon the earth. The promise was made to Israel about life in the land. Simpson took it as a description of what the indwelling Christ makes possible in ordinary time — not an escape from earth, and not a postponement until heaven, but a quality of daily life that belongs to another country.

Not escape, but transformation

It is worth being clear about what he was not saying. He was not describing a life without difficulty. His own contained a nervous collapse, a heart condition, financial insecurity, the loss of children, public controversy and a dark final illness. Whatever days of heaven upon earth meant to him, it plainly did not mean pleasant circumstances. Nor was he recommending detachment — the spirituality that copes with the world by withdrawing attention from it. Simpson was one of the most engaged men of his generation, running rescue missions and orphanages and sending workers to the hardest places on the map. What he meant was that the ordinary day — the same day, with the same trouble in it — is transformed when it is lived in company with Someone.

Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. ISAIAH 26:3

The peace there is not the absence of trouble but the presence of a settled mind, and the condition is a direction of attention.

Moment by moment

Simpson’s practical counsel centred on the smallness of the unit. We tend to think of the spiritual life in large blocks — a good year, a bad season, a period of dryness. He taught believers to think in moments, because a moment is the only thing anyone can actually manage.

Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. MATTHEW 6:34

The grace supplied is for today, and attempting to face next month’s difficulty with today’s supply is the commonest cause of Christian exhaustion. Simpson pointed out that Israel’s manna could not be stored, and that this was a mercy rather than an inconvenience.

As thy days, so shall thy strength be. DEUTERONOMY 33:25

The habit of turning

The practice he recommended is simple enough to be dismissed and difficult enough to take years. It is the habit of turning inwardly to Christ throughout the day — not extended prayer, but a repeated brief recognition that He is present and available: at the start of a task, in the middle of an interruption, before a difficult conversation, on waking in the night.

Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. PSALM 16:8

Simpson held that this practice, sustained, does more for the quality of a life than any amount of intense but occasional devotion. The person who meets God only in a set half-hour has a religious appointment. The person who has learned to turn has a companion.

Joy as evidence

He gave joy a prominent place, and treated its absence as a symptom worth investigating rather than a temperament to be accepted.

These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full. JOHN 15:11

Note whose joy it is. Not a joy we manufacture about our circumstances — His joy, remaining in us. Which means it is not dependent on our circumstances being joyful, and it survives conditions that would extinguish anything we generated ourselves. A caution, though, and Simpson’s own last years supply it. He passed through a period of genuine spiritual darkness at the end of his life, and his friends found it painful to watch in a man who had taught so many about victory. That should be said honestly. Believers experience depression, illness of the mind, and long stretches of dryness, and it is not always a spiritual failure to be corrected. Sometimes it is a burden to be borne, with help, and God does not love such a person less.

The invitation of this chapter is modest and immediate. Not a better year. Today — this afternoon, the next hour — lived in company with Christ.

The discipline of thanksgiving

If one practice above others changes the texture of an ordinary day, Simpson held it was deliberate thanksgiving — and he treated it as a discipline rather than a mood.

In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:18

Two things about that command are worth noticing. It is a command, which means it is not conditional on feeling grateful. We can give thanks in the absence of the sensation, and the sensation often follows the practice rather than preceding it. And it is in every thing, not for every thing. Simpson was careful here, because the distinction protects the sufferer. We are not required to call evil good, to describe a bereavement as a blessing, or to pretend that a diagnosis is welcome. We are required to find God present in the middle of it, and to say so.

I will bless the Lord at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth. PSALM 34:1

The practical form he recommended was specific rather than general. Vague gratitude for blessings in the abstract does very little; naming three particular things, out loud, does a surprising amount — and it works best on the days when the list is hardest to assemble. He connected this directly to the theme of the chapter. Heaven is a place of unbroken thanksgiving. A believer who is learning the habit now is not merely improving his mood; he is practising the native language of the country he is travelling to.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Practise turning inwardly to Christ at three fixed points tomorrow: before work, at a meal, and before something you are dreading. 2. Stop trying to face next month with today’s grace. Ask only for today. 3. When joy is absent, investigate rather than accepting it as your personality — and if the darkness persists, seek help without shame. 4. Take one dull, ordinary hour and consciously invite Christ into it. Notice what changes and what does not. 5. Read Deuteronomy 33:25 slowly on a day when your strength feels inadequate for what is ahead.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have been waiting for a better season, and You have offered me this afternoon.
Teach me to turn to You in the small units — the interruption, the awkward conversation, the tiredness at three o’clock — rather than saving You for a set half hour.
Let Your joy remain in me, not a cheerfulness I have to manufacture.

His own contained a nervous collapse, a heart condition, financial insecurity, the loss of children, public controversy and a dark final illness. Nor was he recommending detachment — the spirituality that copes with the world by withdrawing attention from it. Simpson was one of the most engaged men of his generation, running rescue missions and orphanages and sending workers to the hardest places on the map. What he meant was that the ordinary day — the same day, with the same trouble in it — is transformed when it is lived in company with Someone. A believer who is learning the habit now is not merely improving his mood; he is practising the native language of the country he is travelling to. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Practise turning inwardly to Christ at three fixed points tomorrow: before work, at a meal, and before something you are dreading. 2. Stop trying to face next month with today’s grace. Ask only for today. 3. When joy is absent, investigate rather than accepting it as your personality — and if the darkness persists, seek help without shame. 4. Take one dull, ordinary hour and consciously invite Christ into it. Notice what changes and what does not. 5. fields.body_html:
Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me. MATTHEW 25:40

In the autumn of 1881, A. B. Simpson asked the Thirteenth Street Presbyterian Church in New York to receive into membership a group of Italian immigrants who had been converted through his ministry. The congregation declined. He resigned. He was thirty-seven, with a family to support, and he gave up a distinguished pulpit, a settled salary and the denomination in which he had been raised and ordained. He had no congregation to go to and no income arranged. Everything he built afterwards grew out of that refusal.

The gospel and the unwanted

The conviction behind it had been forming for years. In Louisville he had built a plain tabernacle rather than a handsome church, on the reasoning that working men who owned no respectable clothes would not come where they would be conspicuous. It was a small architectural decision with a large theology behind it.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor. LUKE 4:18

Simpson observed that the churches of his day were arranged, without anyone having decided it, for people like themselves. Pew rents, respectable dress, a manner of speech and an unspoken social threshold combined to make the gospel inaccessible to precisely the people it had first been preached to. He regarded this as a direct violation of an apostolic command.

My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons …Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? JAMES 2:1, 4

James’s example is a congregation that seats a well-dressed visitor comfortably and leaves a poor one standing. Simpson’s point was that we no longer do this crudely, and do it all the time.

What he actually built

The Gospel Tabernacle became a working demonstration. Around it grew rescue missions for the destitute, work among prostitutes, an orphanage, homes where the sick could stay and be cared for and prayed over, and services conducted in the languages of the immigrants pouring into the city. None of this replaced preaching. Simpson would have regarded the suggestion as absurd; he was preaching several times a week and writing continuously throughout. But he did not regard practical mercy as a separate department either, or as a means to secure a hearing for the real message. It was part of the message.

Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. JAMES 1:27

Both, and neither reduced

There is a caution to state, because the century after Simpson divided badly on exactly this point. One wing of the church reduced Christianity to social improvement and quietly lost the gospel of the cross, until it had nothing to offer anyone that a competent charity could not offer better. Another wing reacted by treating practical mercy with suspicion, as a distraction from soul-winning — and produced congregations that could explain justification and would not have noticed a hungry family in the next street. Simpson held both without apparent strain, and the reason is his Fourfold Gospel. A Christ who saves the soul, sanctifies the character, heals the body and is coming to reign over the earth cannot be confined to any single department of human need. The whole person is in view, and so is the whole world.

Whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? 1 JOHN 3:17

The identification

The text at the head of this chapter contains the sharpest claim in the New Testament about the poor, and Simpson took it at face value. The King does not say that serving the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner is like serving Him, or that He approves of it. He says it was done to Him. There is an identification here so complete that the people in the parable are astonished — in both directions. Neither group knew.

For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in. MATTHEW 25:35

The uncomfortable question raised by Simpson’s resignation is not whether your church would refuse a group of immigrant converts. Almost none would say so. It is subtler than that. Who, in practice, is not here? Look around your congregation and ask which kinds of people are absent, and whether anything about the arrangements — the assumptions, the dress, the vocabulary, the unspoken thresholds — helps to explain it.

Money

Simpson’s convictions about the poor were expensive, and it is worth saying how he handled money, because that is where such convictions are tested. He resigned a comfortable salary with a family to support and never again held a position with guaranteed income. The Alliance operated on faith lines: no salaries promised, no debt incurred, and no appeals of the ordinary kind. Money came in and went out, and the needs were made known chiefly to God. Whether every ministry should be run this way is a fair question, and Scripture does not require it — Paul accepted support and asked for it plainly. What is not optional is the underlying attitude, and Simpson’s practice illustrates it.

Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God …that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. 1 TIMOTHY 6:17–18

He held up the Macedonian churches as the pattern, and the details of Paul’s description are pointed: they were in deep poverty, their giving was beyond their means, they had to beg for the privilege, and the sequence began with giving themselves to the Lord first.

For to their power, I bear record, yea, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves. 2 CORINTHIANS 8:3

Note that they were the poor giving to the poor. Simpson observed that generosity is not a function of surplus, and that congregations which wait for prosperity before becoming generous generally discover that prosperity does not produce it either. The test is not the amount but the effect. Giving that does not alter how you live has not yet begun.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look honestly at who is absent from your congregation, and ask what in your arrangements might account for it. 2. Identify one person in your regular orbit whom you have quietly filed as not worth your time. Change that this week. 3. Do something practical and unremarkable for someone who cannot repay you and will not report it. 4. Check which reduction you drift towards — gospel without mercy, or mercy without gospel — and correct in the other direction. 5. Read Matthew 25:31–46 and let the astonishment of both groups do its work. Neither knew.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were anointed to preach the gospel to the poor, and I have built a religion that is comfortable for people like me.
Forgive the respect of persons that I have never had to name because everyone around me shares it.
Show me who is missing, and why. Show me the person I have quietly decided is not worth my attention.
You said it was done to You. Let me believe that this week, in something small and unrecorded. Amen.

fields.title: The Missionary Heart
fields.body_html:
And how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent? ROMANS 10:14–15

Simpson wanted to go to China. His family circumstances prevented it, and he never went anywhere as a missionary. So he spent the rest of his life sending other people, and by the time he died there were several hundred of them scattered across places he had prayed for by name and never seen.

The obligation is the whole church’s

His starting conviction was that the Great Commission was not addressed to specialists.

Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. MATTHEW 28:19

In Simpson’s day, foreign missions was largely the concern of denominational boards, staffed by highly trained men, funded through official channels, and regarded by most ordinary church members as something other people did. He thought this arrangement had no scriptural basis and was producing a fraction of the workers required. His alternative was to make missions the business of the whole church — every member either going, sending, or praying, and none exempt.

Practical machinery

What distinguishes Simpson from other men with the same burden is that he built the machinery. He founded a training school in 1882 — the first Bible institute in North America — on a deliberately unconventional principle. Seven years of classical education was an insuperable barrier for most people with a genuine call, and Simpson judged that it was not necessary. Give ordinary believers a thorough grounding in the Scriptures and practical training, in about two years, and get them to the field. The idea was widely criticised as lowering the standard. It has since been copied by nearly every Bible college in the world. He also organised the sending. The Alliance operated on faith lines — no guaranteed salaries, no debt, no appeals for money in the ordinary sense — and it prioritised what Simpson called the neglected fields: places where no one else was working.

Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man’s foundation. ROMANS 15:20

That verse governed his strategy. Where the gospel had already gone, others could build. The Alliance would go where nobody was.

The cost, stated honestly

It should not be presented as a romance. It was not. Workers went to regions where the mortality rate for foreigners was appalling, and a significant number of them died within a few years, some within months, of disease. Others returned broken. Families were separated for years at a time, and children were sent home to be raised by relatives. The graves are real, and they are in the places Simpson prayed for. He knew the arithmetic and kept sending, and the workers kept going. Whatever one makes of that, it is not the record of people playing at religion.

And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death. REVELATION 12:11

Everyone is in one of three categories

Simpson’s practical challenge to a congregation was that there is no fourth option. You are going — taking the gospel yourself to a people who do not have it, whether across the world or across your own city. You are sending — funding, at a level that affects how you live, the people who go. You are praying — specifically, by name, for workers and for countries, and continuing when nothing appears to happen. Most of us, examined honestly, are doing none of the three and assuming we are covered by general approval of the enterprise.

Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. ISAIAH 6:8

There is one more thing worth noticing about Simpson’s missionary passion, and it connects back to the first chapter of this book. It was not fuelled by guilt, or by statistics, or by a sense of Western obligation. It was fuelled by the conviction that Christ is worthy — that a Person this glorious ought to be known everywhere, and that any nation which does not know Him has been robbed.

Missions, on that understanding, is not chiefly rescue. It is worship extended.

The nearest field

Simpson’s missionary vision began at his own door, and the order in the commission is worth attending to.

And ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. ACTS 1:8

Four circles, and the first is the city you are standing in. Simpson never treated the last as a substitute for the first. The same conviction that sent workers to inland China opened rescue missions a few streets from his own pulpit, and he would have regarded a congregation that supported missionaries abroad while ignoring the neglected nearby as having misread the verse. He also noticed the middle term. Samaria, for a first-century Jerusalem believer, meant the people group next door that one avoided — close in geography and distant in sympathy. Every place has its Samaria, and it is usually the field the local church is least willing to enter, precisely because proximity makes the prejudice harder to disguise. There is a development of this that Simpson saw beginning in New York and that has since transformed the picture. The nations were arriving. Immigrants from countries closed to missionaries were living within walking distance of churches that were praying for those countries and ignoring their citizens.

And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; that they should seek the Lord. ACTS 17:26–27

Paul’s argument is that God arranges where peoples live, and does it with a purpose. If that is true, the presence of a diaspora community in your town is not an accident of economics. It is an assignment.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Determine which of the three you actually are — going, sending, praying — and be honest if the answer is none. 2. If you send, examine whether the amount affects how you live. If it does not, it is not yet sending in the New Testament sense. 3. Adopt one unreached people or one worker, and pray by name for a year.

4. Ask whether anything prevents you from going that is a preference rather than an obstacle. 5. Let the motive be Christ’s worthiness rather than guilt. Guilt does not last; worship does.

A PRAYER
Lord of the harvest, I have approved of missions and contributed almost nothing to them.
I am not going, I am barely sending, and I do not pray for anyone by name. Forgive me for calling that a missionary heart.
Show me which of the three You are asking of me, and let me not negotiate.
And let the reason be Your worthiness — that You are too glorious to remain unknown among any people on earth. Amen.

fields.title: Till He Comes

And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come. MATTHEW 24:14

Everything in Simpson’s life converged on one verse, and it is the one at the head of this chapter. He read it as a task with a stated relation to the return of Christ, and it made him incapable of rest. The gospel is to reach all nations; then the end comes. The work is unfinished; therefore go.

A task with an end in view

Simpson’s contemporaries who shared this conviction expressed it in a phrase that became the watchword of a generation: the evangelisation of the world in this generation. They believed it might be done, and done soon. It was not. A century and more later the task remains unfinished, and the confident timetables of the 1890s look naive. But the failure of the schedule does not touch the substance, and this is worth being clear about. The Lord did not say when. He said that it would happen, and He gave the command in the same breath as the promise of His presence.

Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. MATTHEW 28:20

The believer’s business is not to calculate the completion date. It is to be found working when it arrives.

The end that is certain

What kept Simpson from despair at the size of the task was that he knew how it finishes. It is described, and the description is not ambiguous.

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands. REVELATION 7:9

Every nation. Every language. A multitude beyond counting. That is not a hope that the mission might succeed; it is a report of its outcome.

Which means the missionary enterprise is not a gamble. It is participation in something already certain. The only open question is who will have the privilege of being involved.

Hastening the day

There is a striking phrase in Peter that Simpson took seriously and that most readers pass over.

Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God. 2 PETER 3:12

The margin of many Bibles renders it hastening the coming of that day. The idea that the church’s obedience bears some relation to the timing of the end is difficult, and Christians have understood it differently. But Peter places it immediately after a statement about God’s patience — that He is not willing that any should perish — which suggests the connection is precisely the one Simpson drew.

The Lord is not slack concerning his promise …but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. 2 PETER 3:9

The delay is mercy. It exists so that people still outside may come in. Which is an argument for urgency and against impatience at the same time.

How it ended for him

Simpson’s last years were hard. He grew frail and confused, passed through a season of spiritual darkness that distressed those who loved him, and stepped back from the movement he had founded. He died at Nyack on the twenty-ninth of October, 1919, at seventy-five. He had spent nearly forty years telling people the King was coming soon. The King did not come in his lifetime, and Simpson died the way everyone does. He left no money. He left a training school, a magazine, a hymnbook, a tabernacle full of poor people, and several hundred workers on fields he had never visited. The movement that grew from it is now largely made up of people in the countries he prayed for, and is considerably larger outside his own than within it. He asked for that, and he did not see it, and it happened anyway.

Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:58

The last word of the Bible on this subject is a request, and then a reply.

He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. REVELATION 22:20

Simpson spent his life on the interval between those two sentences. So do we all. The only question is what we do with it.

Living backward from that day

Simpson often urged his hearers to make decisions from the far end — to ask not what seems best now, but what will seem best then.

For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:10

This is not the judgment that determines salvation, which for the believer was settled at the cross. It is the assessment of a life’s work, and Paul describes it elsewhere as a fire that tests what each has built.

If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:14–15

Two things follow, and Simpson held both. There is real security. He himself shall be saved — the believer whose work does not survive is not thereby lost. Nothing in this doctrine should produce terror in someone trusting Christ. And there is real seriousness. It is possible to spend a Christian life on things that will not last, and to arrive with very little to show for a great deal of activity. Simpson thought most of us are in more danger of this than of gross sin, because it requires no decision — only drift. The practical exercise he suggested is to project forward. Consider the thing occupying most of your energy at present, and ask honestly whether you expect to be glad of it on that day. Then consider the thing you keep postponing — the reconciliation, the giving, the going — and ask the same question. The answers are usually available immediately, which is itself instructive.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Stop waiting for a clearer sense of the timetable. The command was given without one. 2. Take up one piece of unfinished work — a person, a place, a task — and commit to it for a year rather than a week.

3. Let Revelation 7:9 settle your discouragement. The outcome is reported, not hoped for. 4. Treat the delay as mercy for those not yet in, and let that shape how you speak of the world’s condition. 5. Ask what you would want to be doing when He appears, and begin doing more of it this week.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You said the gospel would reach all nations, and then the end would come. I have believed that and lived as though it had nothing to do with me.
The task is unfinished. Show me my part of it, and let me not wait for certainty about the timing that You have declined to give.
Thank You that the outcome is not in doubt — that there will be a multitude from every nation and tongue before Your throne, and that no labour spent on that is wasted.
Keep me steadfast to the end. Even so, come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Christ is all, and in all. COLOSSIANS 3:11

Eighteen chapters can make it appear that A. B. Simpson taught a great many things. He taught one thing, and everything else is that one thing applied. The one thing is this: Christ Himself is the supply for every need a human being has, and He supplies it not by sending something but by being Someone within us. Follow it through and the whole structure appears. Christ our Saviour — He does not merely provide salvation, He is it, and He enters. Christ our Sanctifier — holiness is not achieved but received, because it is a Person. Christ our Healer — the same indwelling life reaching the body. Christ our Coming King — the Person we have received is the Person we shall see. The self life goes because the Christ life comes. The Spirit’s whole work is to make this Christ real. Faith is how He is taken; prayer is fellowship with Him; the Scriptures are about Him; an ordinary Tuesday becomes a day of heaven because He is in it. And the reason to cross an ocean is that He is too glorious to remain unknown. Four wheels, one chariot, one Person.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, you are in some danger, and Simpson would have named it before anyone. The peculiar risk of deeper-life teaching is that it can generate exactly the condition it was written to cure. A person reads about the fullness, the surrender, the land of promise — and sets off in pursuit of an experience. He attends the meeting, makes the consecration, has the feeling, and is empty six weeks later. So he tries again, and the cycle that Simpson escaped becomes the cycle this book has installed. The whole point of his hymn is that the pursuit ends when the object changes. Not the blessing but the Lord. Not the feeling but the Word. Not the gift but the Giver.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So the plainest counsel this book can give is the same as in its companion volumes. Go back to the chapter that made you least comfortable — not the one you found most interesting. Take its application points and work them slowly over months. Then take the next.

Two things to carry

First, ask for Himself. Not for more of the Spirit, whom you already have. Not for a blessing you can describe. For Christ — and then go about your work without checking your feelings hourly to see whether it took. Second, hold the four wheels together. Simpson’s great gift to the church was proportion. In every generation, ministries are built on one emphasis, and the one emphasis eventually distorts everything else — healing without holiness, prophecy without evangelism, experience without doctrine, doctrine without compassion. Simpson’s answer to the man who wanted him to specialise still stands: there are four wheels on the chariot, and three of them cannot be neglected for one.

A last word about the man

We have been honest about his failures. His teaching on healing has done real damage where it was taken further than Scripture warrants, and some who followed him died of conditions that could have been treated. His confidence that the world might be evangelised in his own generation was mistaken. His framework of sanctification as a distinct crisis is disputed by serious Christians who read the same texts differently. And the man who taught so many about victory ended his own life in frailty, confusion and a season of spiritual darkness that those who loved him found hard to watch. That last fact should not be tidied away, because it is pastorally important. If a man who taught the deeper life for forty years could finish in darkness, then darkness is not proof that someone has failed. It may simply be the end of a long race run by a body that is wearing out. God did not love him less in 1919 than in 1881. None of this has been raised to diminish him. It has been raised because his own theology requires it. A teaching whose whole point is that we have nothing in ourselves and everything in Christ cannot be commended by pretending its teacher was an exception.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

He died at Nyack in the autumn of 1919, having spent forty years telling people that the King was coming soon. The King did not come in his lifetime. He left no money. He left a training school that has been copied on every continent, a hymnbook, a magazine, a tabernacle full of the sort of people other churches did not want, and several hundred workers in countries he had prayed for by name and never visited. The movement that grew out of it is now far larger in those countries than in his own, and is made up overwhelmingly of people who have never heard of him. He asked for exactly that. He did not see it. It happened anyway, which is the ordinary arrangement, and he would not have minded in the least — provided the credit went where it belonged.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have read about Your all-sufficiency, and I am capable of turning even that into one more experience to chase.
Keep me from it. I do not want the blessing; I want You. I do not want a fuller feeling; I want more of me to be Yours.
Be my salvation, my holiness, my strength, and my hope. Hold the four wheels of my life together, so that I do not become a person of one emphasis and no proportion.
And when my own strength fails at the end, as his did, hold me then too. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to A. B. Simpson
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Simpson is easy to read and easy to obtain. He wrote for ordinary congregations rather than for scholars, his sentences are short, and his illustrations are plain. Everything he published is now in the public domain and a great deal of it is freely available online. The difficulty is the opposite of the one Edwards presents. Simpson wrote a great deal, quickly, often for a weekly deadline, and the quality is uneven. Some volumes repeat one another. The guide below is arranged to save the reader time.

Begin here

The Fourfold Gospel. Short, and the best single entry point. The whole framework in a few dozen pages. The Self Life and the Christ Life. His most searching practical book, and the basis of chapter six of this volume. If a reader wants to be uncomfortable in a useful way, this is the one. Days of Heaven Upon Earth. A daily devotional, still in print after more than a century. The gentlest introduction to him and a good gift.

On the deeper life

Wholly Sanctified. A small book on 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Clear, warm and practical. The Land of Promise. His exposition of the Canaan typology treated in chapter eight. A Larger Christian Life. On enlargement of faith, service and expectation. The Christ Life. Brief essays on union with Christ.

On the Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, in two volumes, tracing the Spirit’s work through the Old and New Testaments respectively. Long, but the fullest statement of the teaching in chapters nine and ten. When the Comforter Came. Thirty-one short readings; much more accessible.

On prayer and Scripture

The Life of Prayer. Short and practical. Christ in the Bible. His commentary on the whole Scripture, book by book, in many volumes, asking of each where Christ is found. Not to be read through; to be consulted alongside whatever you are studying. The Names of Jesus. A study of the titles of Christ.

Approach with care

The Gospel of Healing (1885). The fullest statement of the teaching treated in chapter four of this book, and the volume that requires the cautions set out there. Simpson’s own practice of setting aside medical means went beyond what Scripture teaches, and readers should not follow him in it. Read it alongside 2 Corinthians 12:7–10 and 2 Timothy 4:20.

The hymns

Simpson wrote more than a hundred, usually to be sung by his own congregation within days of being written. Himself is the essential one and states his whole theology; Jesus Only and Yesterday, Today, Forever are also widely known. They are worth reading as compressed teaching, not merely as devotional verse.

About Simpson

A. W. Tozer’s Wingspread (1943) is the best-known life, written by the Alliance’s most famous son. It is short, admiring, beautifully written, and not a critical biography. A. E. Thompson’s The Life of A. B. Simpson (1920) is the official account, published the year after his death, and valuable for its proximity to the events. Charles Nienkirchen’s A. B. Simpson and the Pentecostal Movement is the standard scholarly treatment of the tongues controversy discussed in chapter ten, and is more critical than the devotional lives. Read more than one. The older biographies are written by people who loved him, and it shows in what they leave out.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. Simpson claimed no authority of his own, and his method was to argue from texts. Check them. Read him for the burden rather than the system. Where he presses a framework beyond what Scripture states — in the healing teaching, in the sanctification crisis, in the expectation of an imminent completion of the missionary task — take the pastoral concern and leave the scaffolding.

And read him slowly. His books are short and can be finished in an evening, which is precisely the danger. A chapter a week, acted on, will do more than the whole shelf admired.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
